PHILADELPHIA — The Giants were headed into their bye week, holding a surprising lead of 1.5 games in the NFC East. The division certainly appeared to be wide open.

What happened with those teams in Week 8 played out completely how the Giants wanted to see it transpire. The Cowboys blew a lead and lost to the Cardinals in overtime. The Eagles' demise continued with a loss to the Commanders in an inter-division tussle between the two bottom-feeders. As they parted ways for a few days to catch their breath and soothe their aching muscles, the Giants (4-2-1) added to their hold on first place.

Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni looks on during the second quarter against the Washington Commanders in Landover, Md., Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. Getty Images

This week, they can further distance themselves from the pack. There is Sunday's meeting with the Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field, otherwise known as the House of Horrors for the Giants. There is a quick turnaround for Thursday night's rematch with the Commanders at MetLife Stadium (they tied the first meeting a month ago in Landover, Md.).

"Not to look ahead to the game on Thursday, this is a pivotal part of our season coming up with two division games that can really help us down the road,'' guard Jon Runyan Jr. told The Post.

No, coach John Harbaugh did not print up "2-0'' shirts to encapsulate the task at hand this week, but he did say after beating the Texans in overtime, "The two most important games of the season will be coming up after the bye, which will set the direction for the rest of the season.''

In the past, this encounter was a litmus test for the Giants, and they usually failed it, miserably — highlighting the gap between the two franchises. Now comes quite a juxtaposition.

The Giants are atop the division and the Eagles (2-6) are at the bottom, mired in a six-game losing streak and without their starting quarterback, Jalen Hurts, for the remainder of the season. They take a flier on Joe Milton III in his first NFL start, and there is talk in Philly about rebuilding and regime change — all the discordant noise the Giants heard about their own situation for the past decade.

New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh answers questions from the media during football practice in East Rutherford, N.J., Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. Noah K. Murray for NY Post

The Giants are actually favored in a building where they have not won since 2013, losers of 13 straight at the Linc. That streak has nothing to do with Harbaugh and nothing to do with J.J. McCarthy, looking to build off his impressive Giants starting debut two weeks ago in Houston. McCarthy likely will be without top running back Cam Skattebo (listed as doubtful with a strained hamstring) and, with Tyrone Tracy Jr. on injured reserve, it will be a makeshift backfield for the Giants.

Still, the Giants are finding ways to win, and that can make a team feel good about itself. And that can sometimes open the door for a whiff of complacency to enter.

"Our leaders have talked to the guys about that,'' Harbaugh said. "We're not really anywhere close to that yet. We're fighting for our lives, too. We've got everything to gain, and we know how big this game is. We know who we're going against. We'll be ready.

"In this league, to even think for one second that something's not going to be a challenge or that you might get complacent or that it might not, what would even be on your mind if you thought that? If you're the right kind of team, it's just like, 'Really, you're asking me that?' Shame on us if we would think that way, and we're not thinking that way.''

The Eagles are battered with injuries and the Giants do not care.

"I mean, we got players down as well,'' cornerback Greg Newsome II said. "We lost our starting quarterback early. We lost our best defensive player in Brian Burns early. Obviously, we got Tremaine [Edmunds]. Our job is to fight that complacency, and I think we got the right guys to do it.''

#2809. IND 2-0 up vs NZ in ODI series: List of teams who have lost a ODI series after taking 2-0 lead

IND 2-0 up vs NZ in ODI series: List of teams who have lost a ODI series after taking 2-0 lead originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

India lead New Zealand 2-0 after two close wins, and history now offers a warning.

Only a handful of teams have thrown away such a lead in a series of five or more matches.

India themselves have suffered this fate once before, and the details may surprise fans.

India head into the third ODI against New Zealand with a 2-0 lead, though cricket history shows that such an advantage is not always the safe position it appears to be. A small group of teams have let a similar lead slip in a bilateral series, and the names on that list include India themselves.

The hosts were beaten in Auckland by five wickets, a result reached under the DLS method, and then lost again in Wellington by four runs, once more through DLS. Those two results have put India in front in the five-match series, and the remaining games will decide whether New Zealand can mount a recovery.

The record books say it has been done only rarely, as a 0-2 deficit has been overturned just five times in ODI series of five or more matches.

The sections below set out who has managed it, how India fell short in the past, and when the rest of the current series will be played.

MORE: Rahul hailed as India clinch a narrow win in Wellington

South Africa have achieved this twice, while Bangladesh, Pakistan and Australia have each done it once. That makes it a very uncommon feat, since it has happened only five times in more than 50 years of men's ODI cricket.

The table below lists the sides that surrendered a 2-0 lead, along with the team that came back.

In 2003, Pakistan took a 2-0 lead at home with wins in Lahore, by 8 runs and then by 42 runs. South Africa answered by winning in Faisalabad by 13 runs and then twice in Rawalpindi, by six wickets and by seven wickets, to take the series 3-2.

Two years later, Zimbabwe won the first two games in Dhaka, by 102 runs and 31 runs. Habibul Bashar's Bangladesh then took the last three, in Dhaka by 40 runs and in Chattogram by 58 runs and eight wickets respectively, to complete a historic turnaround.

In 2016, England went 2-0 up in South Africa after winning in Bloemfontein by 39 runs via DLS, and in Port Elizabeth, by five wickets. AB de Villiers' side then won at Centurion by seven wickets, in Johannesburg by one wicket and in Cape Town by five wickets.

MORE: Rahul vs Axar at No. 5: Why India should prefer Rahul in SENA conditions and 2027 WC

India have lost a series after leading 2-0 on two occasions, and this will be a familiar story for many supporters. The most recent was in 2019, when Virat Kohli's team went ahead after wins in Hyderabad, by six wickets, and Nagpur, by eight runs.

Aaron Finch's Australia then took charge, helped by Usman Khawaja's centuries, and won in Ranchi by 32 runs, in Mohali by four wickets and in Delhi by 35 runs.

India's other collapse from a 2-0 position came in the six-match home series against Pakistan in April 2005. The hosts began strongly, winning the opener in Kochi by 87 runs after posting 281/8, and then taking the second game at Visakhapatnam by 58 runs, when their total of 356/9 proved too much for a Pakistan side that finished on 298.

The visitors hit back in Jamshedpur, where they scored 319/9 and won by 106 runs, and they stayed in control at Ahmedabad, where a rain-shortened 48-over game ended with Pakistan reaching 319/7 in pursuit of 316 and winning by three wickets. They then chased a target of 250 at Kanpur, finishing on 252/5 in 42.1 overs, before sealing the series 4-2 in Delhi, where they made 303/8 and restricted India to 144 in 37 overs to win by 159 runs.

#2805. 5 key numbers from Iowa football's 24-10 win over Northwestern

Iowa football moved to 7-2 overall and 4-2 in the Big Ten after getting a 24-10 win at Northwestern on Nov. 7, keeping the Hawkeyes' College Football Playoff hopes alive.

Iowa set the tone early in the game, getting a touchdown on its first drive of the game. The defense stuffed a Wildcats offense that was without its starting quarterback, Aiden Chiles.

It was the first loss for Northwestern in brand-new Ryan Field, and Iowa's fifth straight win over the Wildcats.

Here are five numbers that tell the story of the win for the Hawkeyes.

Hank Brown scored Iowa's first touchdown on the opening drive, taking off on a quarterback draw from 21 yards out.

This was Brown's second rushing touchdown of the season, the first coming against Iowa State in Week 2.

His final stat line: 16 completions on 21 attempts, 126 yards, one rushing touchdown, one passing touchdown and an interception. He threw the ball over the top of two defenders to Tony Diaz for a second-quarter touchdown.

Jackson returned a kickoff for a touchdown for the second time this season. He caught the ball at the 4-yard line, found his blockers and picked up speed as he beat out Northwestern defenders to score. Jackson was untouched during the entire run.

Jackson had a 99-yard kickoff return for a touchdown against Michigan, helping the Hawkeyes earn a 20-19 victory in Ann Arbor.

Phillips had a strong game on the ground as he took on a bulk of the carries for the Hawkeyes.

After starting the season slowly due to injury, he stepped up for the team with Kamari Moulton out for the season. Phillips picked up 128 yards on 21 carries (6.1 average), including a 45-yard run that moved the ball from Iowa's 7-yard line to midfield. That was the key play on a 97-yard scoring drive.

Iowa ball-carriers racked up 170 rushing yards on 33 carries (5.2 average).

Iowa's defense played another great game and has been sharp since the Oct. 16 bye week. Phil Parker's group held opponents without a point for 100 minutes 46 seconds of game clock before Northwestern's field goal in the third quarter on Saturday.

A big part of the unit's success in Evanston was getting to Northwestern's Nicco Marchiol six times.

Jayden Montgomery, Bryce Hawthorne, Drew Campbell, Luke Gaffney, Kenneth Merriweather and Iose Espenesa each brought down the Wildcats quarterback.

Cam Buffington led the defense with 12 tackles.

The Wildcats went 1-for-11 on third down in the loss. They punted the ball away five times.

Iowa was 7-of-13 on third down. The Hawkeye defense held Northwestern to 286 yards and 4.1 yards per play.

#2800. Louisville Defeats Georgia Tech, 44-17

Despite the odd start with special teams blunders, I think most would agree this was the most complete performance of the season thus far.

This team has had similar blow out wins against FSU and Stanford, but in those games it took a minute for the team to hit the gas a turn away. But in this one it never felt like Georgia Tech was in the game.

After scoring on the first drive, the defense had to force multiple 3-and-outs to start their game before they finally conceded 3 points thanks to the special teams. Brohm looked as equally as frustrated as the rest of us, but it didn't last long as the offense looked unstoppable and the defense looked….good?

The game in its entirety was as close to perfect as fans have been hoping for all season, and for it to come in November when there's still 3 very important games ahead could not be better timing.

Lincoln looked in control all game as he finished 17/25 for 182 yds and 2 TDs, to go along with his 81 yards on the ground. Treyshun Hurry did a fantastic job filling in for the injured McCoy as he reeled in 8 receptions for 104 yards and a TD. The Brown Bros. rushed for a modest combined total of 92 yards on just 16 carries against one of, if not the worst rushing defenses in the conference. But it didn't matter as the offense got pretty much whatever they wanted.

And I'd be remiss if I didn't mention this gorgeous jet sweep to Tre Richardson for a 52-yard TD, his second of the night.

Meanwhile on the defense they made life hell for whoever was playing QB tonight. Tech couldn't seem to figure out what would work between Mendoza and Adamson, and it wasn't much of anything between the two.

The defense held Ga. Tech to an outstanding 4 of 17 on 3rd down, and 5.4 yards per pass and just 3.4 yards per rush. But the biggest numbers of the night came from the defensive front as they had 4 sacks, 7 TFLs, and 5 batted balls. It seemed like even when the commitee of QBs got time to throw, there was either pressure coming and/or hands blocking throwing lanes.

It was a fantastic effort from the defense and one that I think we all hope the team can build on as they entire the final quarter of the season with a lot left on the table.

It's not often you get to kick your feet up and watch your team trounce a conference foe while other certain teams are getting blown out. So enjoy nights like tonight. We've all earned this one.

Saraf, now in his second year after being drafted in the first round of the 2025 NBA draft, didn't deliver the shooting performance you'd expect.

The 20-year-old finished with eight points on 3-of-14 shooting, including a rough 1-of-8 outing from beyond the arc. Entering this season, the biggest question surrounding Saraf's game was if he could find consistency from 3-point range.

Despite those struggles, however, he still managed to impact the game as a facilitator. The 6'6" 20-year-old guard dished out seven assists, which led the team. That's what makes him interesting. When his shot isn't falling, he can create chances for his teammates, but that also comes with turnovers, and he committed three in 32 minutes. But a 2.3-to-1 assist ration is seen as a very good number in the NBA.

His passing ability has been known. The next step in his development, though, is developing into at least a respectable scoring threat. The Nets' backcourt in Brooklyn is a logjam, especially with Nolan Traoré's strong play to open the season.

For Saraf to get his chance in the NBA this season, he'll need to be more than a facilitator.

The only other member of the Flatbush 5 who played on Friday was Powell. Like Saraf, the UNC product had a tough night on offense.

Powell tallied just six points on 2-of-6 shooting in 25 minutes, missing all three deep attempts. Despite the rough night, he managed four rebounds, three assists, a steal, and a block.

Similarly to Saraf's game, though, that was nothing new. Powell's defensive potential has been the most promising element of his game, given the length and athleticism he boasts with a 6'6″ frame and a 7-foot wingspan, ideal for a defender. He showed that facet of his profile again vs. Greensboro.

However, his offense remains a work-in-progress, at best. During Summer League, the 22nd pick in 2025 pick struggled mightily with his jump shot, shooting a brutal 1-for-28 from the field, including zero makes on 14 deep attempts.

If he can develop into a reliable catch-and-shoot option while becoming someone who can defend multiple positions at the NBA level, that's a valuable player. Coming away with a legitimate 3-and-D guy at the 22nd overall pick would be a really nice win for the Nets towards the end of the first round.

The issue, though, is that he is now in Year 2 and doesn't look particularly close to becoming that type of player. For someone with his defensive tools, even mild offensive improvements would make a big difference.

Obviously the upside is there, but Powell has to start putting the pieces together.

Perhaps the most exciting part from Friday was simply getting an extended look at Joshua Jefferson. After all, it's been a long time coming.

He was selected with the 28th pick in June's draft, a byproduct of the Julius Randle-for-Nic Claxton trade, and played minimally throughout Summer League as thst trade took until the eve of Summer League to be finalized. He couldn't even practice with his Nets teammates. Then, he missed Brooklyn's preseason due to a lower back injury.

Given all of that, Friday was the first real look that fans got on the Iowa State product, and he didn't disappoint, coming away with 15 points, six rebounds, and three assists, shooting 5-of-9 overall and 3-of-7 from three. Not a bad first impression.

Standing at 6'9" and 240 pounds, Jefferson stands out because he is very well-rounded and brings a little bit of everything to the table, hence his solid box score. There's always a role for someone like that in the NBA, especially with the size that he offers. It's why the term "point forward" was commonly used to describe him throughout the pre-draft process.

Given the abundance of wings up in Brooklyn, it's going to be tough for him to crack the NBA rotation right away, but Friday was a strong showing in the first-round rookie's first legitimate chance.

If there was one thing the Nets knew they were getting when they selected Bilodeau with the 43rd overall pick in June's draft, it was his shooting ability.

Throughout 64 games at UCLA in two seasons, he shot a whopping 43.8% from three-point range. It was on a significant sample size, too, attempting 233 threes as a Bruin. His 46.0% last season was the highest of any player taken in the 2026 Draft.

While it's just one game, that skill was on full display during Long Island's opener. The UCLA product finished with 13 points, four rebounds, two assists, and five steals, while shooting 5-of-10 from the field and 3-of-7 from deep.

Beyond the shooting, though, what jumps off the page is his five steals in 25 minutes. With that outing, he became the first Long Island Net in franchise history, dating back to 2016, to log five steals in a G League debut.

That matters because one of the biggest concerns about Bilodeau's game coming out of college was his defense. So seeing him make such a noticeable impact on that end right away matters…

Speaking with NetsDaily at Long Island's Media Day last week, he emphasized how much he feels his game has already grown since Summer League, adding that defense has been "a big improvement."

"I feel like I've improved so much since Summer League," the No. 43 pick said. "I think a big improvement of mine has been defensively, trusting myself a little more, and getting used to guarding the perimeter. I didn't do much of that last year."

Obviously, Bilodeau's top trait is shooting, and when he gets his opportunity in Brooklyn, it'll most likely be because of that calling card. But at 6'8" and 228 pounds, he certainly has the size to blossom into at least a serviceable defender, and Friday was a step in that direction for him.

Grant Nelson's start to the season on Friday is exactly what he needed to get off on the right foot. The 24-year-old finished with 18 points and 13 rebounds, including six offensive boards while shooting 8-of-16 from the field in 27 minutes.

He missed all five attempts from beyond the arc, which isn't ideal, but it was promising to see strong overall scoring output and activity on the glass as well as a willingness to take the deep shot. The Alabama product also used his size and athleticism on defense, coming away with a block and a steal.

The shots didn't go his way, especially from deep, but that's an area of his game Nelson spent a lot of time developing during his rehabilitation after patellar tendinitis cut his season short last year.

"I think it's extremely important with the direction that the game has been going in," he told us at Media Day. "I mean, I think it's just adding another part to my game, being versatile in that way. Most bigs can shoot now. So being able to do that, I think it will definitely help me out in my career."

At 7'0", Nelson is fascinating because he offers the exact tools that the Nets could potentially need in Brooklyn. With his athleticism, he brings a little bit of everything, but most notably rim protection ability, which Long Island's parent club currently lacks.

Proving that he deserves an NBA chance, though, especially on a crowded roster, starts with taking advantage of his chances with Long Island, which Friday was an example of. Now he must build on that.

Long Island is back in action Saturday night against the Swarm, then faces the College Park Skyhawks, the Hawks affiliate on Tuesday, before their home opener Friday against College Park at the Nassau Coliseum.

#2787. 6 moments that defined Rob Gronkowski’s Patriots career

Rob Gronkowski is a New England Patriots Hall of Famer, and it is not hard to see why. Not only was he an integral part of the organization's Dynasty 2.0 in the 2010s, he also performed at the highest level throughout his nine seasons with the team.

When he left the Patriots after the 2018 season — one capped by his third championship — he did so as the owner of 15 NFL records. While some of those have been broken over the last seven years, his impact on the Patriots and the NFL as a whole is undeniable.

Breaking it down to a handful of moments is therefore a challenging task. This collection is therefore more of a "greatest hits" than a comprehensive journey through his oeuvre.

Despite questions about a back injury and even though he fell asleep during his pre-draft visit to Gillette Stadium, the Patriots forced their luck in the second round of the 2010 NFL Draft. Trading up two spots to leap-frog the Baltimore Ravens, they secured Gronkowski with the 42nd overall selection. That moment, which saw him celebrate on stage with his entire immediate family, already set the tone for what was about to come.

Coming off a solid rookie season, Gronkowski fully broke out in Year 2 to establish himself as the best tight end in the NFL and a player with sky-high potential. There were multiple plays during his impressive 2011 campaign that can be picked as examples, but one stands out above the rest: a 49-yard catch-and-run against Washington that showed his rare blend of speed, power and elusiveness. It was one of the first times in his career that he showed that he was a different animal.

Even with Peyton Manning gone, Patriots vs. Colts was still one of the NFL's best rivalries in the mid-2010s. And one particular matchup stands out in regards to Gronkowski: Week 11 of the 2014 season. He finished the game with a non-conspicuous stat-line of four catches, 71 yards and a touchdown. That score, however, was arguably the most spectacular one of his nine-year career: like a "runaway track," as Al Michaels said on the broadcast, he ran over defenders on his way to turning a short third-down conversion into a 26-yard score. Of course, his performance that day was also remembered for something else.

A true tight end, Gronkowski was a dual-impact player both due to his immense receiving prowess and his abilities as a blocker. His contributions in the second area oftentimes go undervalued, but they also define who he was as a player: a powerful and physical presence at the point of attack. Him blocking standout edge Terrell Suggs 1-on-1 in the 2011 AFC Championship Game is a prime example of that, and so is one of the most re-watched moments of his career, when he threw Colts safety Sergio Brown "out of the club" in 2014.

A large part of Gronkowski's success as a Patriots was not just his physical superiority over his opponents, but also his ability to be on the same page as his quarterback; it is why Tom Brady made sure to recruit him to Tampa Bay to close out both players' careers. The chemistry between the two was on constant display for nine years, but if we had to choose one moment as an example — despite the eventual unsatisfactory outcome — it would be the 2015 AFC Championship Game in Denver. Going against a generational defense, Gronkowski converted two massive fourth downs in the late fourth quarter.

Gronkowski's Patriots story cannot be told without also mentioning the injuries he had to overcome, and his Super Bowl history reflects that. He was severely limited against the Giants in 2012 and unable to play against the Falcons in 2017; he also did have a profound impact on the game in his three other appearances, including, in Super Bowl LIII. That particular game put a perfect bow on his career with the team. Slowed by years of physical challenges, he still managed one last hurrah against the Rams: going up the seam as part of the New England's famous Hoss-Y-Juke concept, he hauled in the biggest catch of the game — one that helped set up the only touchdown in the Patriots' eventual 13-3 victory. It was Gronkowski's final catch as a Patriot, and a worthy send-off.

What additional moments do you think defined Gronkowski's career with the Patriots? Please head down to the comment section to share your choices with the community.

How do you know when a football coach is lying? If he’s good at it, you don’t.

Because they all do. Particularly in so-called “must-lie” situations.

There’s an art to it. A way to conceal a lie with another lie. On Friday, Eagles coach Nick Sirianni opted not to lie about the fact that he lied on Monday when he told reporters that quarterback Tanner McKee would not be benched.

“Tanner’s our guy,” Sirianni said. “We’re not making any changes there.”

On Wednesday, the Eagles made a change there, elevating Joe Milton over McKee. The move was announced after Sirianni had his midweek media availability, which prevented him from being asked questions about the change in position from “Tanner’s our guy” to “Tanner’s not our guy.”

On Friday, Sirianni finally faced the music regarding his comments from Monday. In lieu of coming up with an explanation premised on the idea that what he said was true when he said it and circumstances changed, Sirianni surprisingly admitted that he wasn’t telling the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth to reporters and, in turn, the fans.

“I was going to hold onto that as long as I possibly could, every second, every minute,” Sirianni said. “Again, I’m not real shy with you guys. I’m going to tell you what I want to tell you guys. I respect the job that y’all have to do, but I’m going to tell you what I want to tell you guys because I’m always going to protect the team first and foremost.

“Every second that goes by in a situation like that, that you can hold onto information as long as you possibly can, is a little less time for the opponent to get ready for the game. I know there’s a lot of interest in everything that you all want to hear, the fans want to hear. My job is to win football games, do everything we can do to help win football games, protect the guys here on this football team, and handle everything that I can inside.”

In an industry where the truth is only told when it’s coincidental to strategic interests, it’s jarring that Sirianni told the truth that he was lying. It would have been easy to say, “We took a more careful look at the situation after Monday.” Or, even more simply, “We changed our mind. Shit happens.”

Instead, Sirianni opted to say, essentially, “Bullshit happens.” Instead of bothering to concoct a cover story regarding his lie, he said, essentially, “Yeah. I lied. I’ll do it whenever I feel like I have to.”

That’s the most important thing to remember. Coaches lie whenever they feel like they have to. Despite that fact, reporters and fans routinely take their words at face value, swallowing the bullshit while saying, “Thank you, sir, may I have another?”

So thank you, Nick, for making my job a little easier. In my first week of law school, one of the professors said, “The most important thing I can do for you is to give you a good crap filter.”

Because crap is everywhere. Usually, the people spewing it don’t admit it. When they do, it provides a tangible reminder as to whatever they say in the future.

For Sirianni, that’s the most problematic aspect of his decision to tell the truth about lying. There’s now an “Exhibit A” to which anyone and everyone can point as to anything and everything he says when assessing whether he’s being straight with reporters and, in turn, with fans.

#2785. Early Homestead Crash Dooms Corey Day’s Title Hopes

Corey Day entered Saturday's NASCAR O'Reilly Auto Parts Series Championship Race 23 points behind leader Justin Allgaier. With 20 extra points being awarded to the winner of the race compared to second place, Day was in contention to win the 2026 championship when the race at Homestead-Miami Speedway began.

The driver of the No. 17 started the 200-lap race from the seventh position. However, the rookie's hopes of winning the title on Saturday night ended almost as quickly as it began.

On Lap 9, Day was racing Rajah Caruth for position. Going down the backstretch, the Hendrick Motorsports driver attempted to clear Caruth for the spot.

Day collided with the outside retaining wall after driving across the nose of Caruth's No. 88 Chevrolet. The damage was significant, causing Day to go to the garage area and make repairs.

While the four-time winner would return to the race, Day ultimately finished 34th, 25 laps down. The sliver of hope Day had to win the championship was dashed quickly in Saturday's season finale.

In the early laps of Saturday's championship race, Day began to get antsy when points leader Justin Allgaier passed him for position.

At that moment, Day felt he needed to make something happen. Unfortunately, the attempt at an aggressive pass on Caruth did not pay off and subsequently doomed his hopes at the 2026 championship.

After the race, Day did not point the finger at Caruth or anyone else. The only person to blame, Day said, was himself.

"I just messed up. Just didn't have the pace I needed on the short run. The 7 (Allgaier) got by me and I needed those points and I just got greedy and wasn't clear and cleared myself. Simple as that. No one did anything wrong besides me," Day said.

Losing the opportunity to win the 2026 championship was not the only price Day paid for crashing in Saturday's O'Reilly Auto Parts Series finale.

Day entered the final race of the season third in the standings. With a difficult 34th-place result, Day dropped from third to fifth in the standings. Carson Kvapil finished the season third in points, while Sheldon Creed ended the season fourth.

Justin Allgaier went on to win the championship, the second of his career and second in the last three years.

Despite the frustrating end, it was still a successful rookie campaign for Day. The 20-year-old out of Clovis, California totaled four wins in 2026 along with 12 top 5s and 22 top 10s.

Day is set to return to Hendrick Motorsports as the driver of the No. 17 in 2027. He will also make part-time Cup Series starts for Spire Motorsports next year.

#2779. Rams listed Matthew Stafford with elbow injury because reporters asked about ice on it

On Monday, reporters asked Rams coach Sean McVay about quarterback Matthew Stafford having ice on his throwing arm after Sunday’s win over the Chargers. On Wednesday, the Rams listed Stafford as having an elbow injury.

“Really, it’s because you guys asked me about it earlier in the week,” McVay told reporters on Friday regarding the decision to disclose an elbow injury for Stafford. “It’s more semantical than anything else. It’s normal, like what he told you guys, but because you guys asked me about him having ice on his elbow. . . . He’s been full, hasn’t missed any sort of reps so normal management stuff that he’s been doing over the last few years.”

It conjures memories of the Patriots’ one-time habit of listing former quarterback Tom Brady as “probable” with a “right shoulder” injury. That all started because he had ice on his shoulder in the locker room, reporters inquired, and the team decided to just put him on the injury report every week.

Has the elbow situation affected Stafford’s throwing?

“I haven’t seen any of that,” McVay said. “I told you guys he’d be better equipped to talk about it. He’s been a full participant, been awesome. He’s spinning the ball. He’s been able to activate all parts of the field with great timing, rhythm, and accuracy so he’s been great.”

So either he has an actual elbow injury that the Rams had been concealing, or he doesn’t really have an elbow injury but they listed him as having one because reporters noticed ice on his arm and asked McVay about it. Neither explanation seems to reflect the true spirit of the injury report, which expects real injuries — and only real injuries — to be disclosed.

Either Stafford has an elbow injury that was previously hidden or he doesn’t have an elbow injury and the claim that he has one is a middle finger to the meddling reporters who were doing their jobs. Neither explanation is a preferred alternative to the unvarnished truth.

#2774. Report: Colts are in trade talks regarding QB Daniel Jones

The Indianapolis fire sale could indeed extend to the man who was supposed to become a franchise quarterback there.

According to ESPNFL, the Colts have engaged in trade talks this week regarding Daniel Jones, speaking to “multiple teams.”

The precise language of the report identifies only one team as actually talking to the Colts. From the article, the Ravens “were one team to check in on Jones.” The Ravens ultimately struck a deal with the Cardinals for quarterback Jacoby Brissett, whose plunge from No. 1 to No. 3 on the depth chart made it clear to the rest of the league that he was available.

The only other team mentioned by name is the Vikings, and the report points only to "[s]peculation” involving Minnesota. (We’ve been “speculating” about it since the immediate aftermath of Sunday’s loss by the Vikings in Detroit.)

Past ESPNFL reporting on a potential trade for running back Jonathan Taylor ultimately listed five teams as talking to the Colts (Giants, Seahawks, Broncos, Packers, Vikings). The fact that other teams weren’t mentioned as to Jones suggests that, frankly, there may not be other teams.

Really, which current contender would want him? The Vikings are the only potential playoff team that checks the box as possibly needing a starter right now. And only the Vikings and Giants are contenders with which Jones has direct experience. (The Giants wouldn’t want a Jones reunion, and Jones surely wouldn’t want it, either.)

That could change this weekend, obviously. One injury to a starter could alter the dynamics, spurring another contender to pick up the phone and make a push for Jones. The most memorable example of that came 15 years ago, when a broken collarbone to Raiders quarterback Jason Campbell prompted a quick deal for Bengals quarterback Carson Palmer, who had decided he didn’t want to play for the team that had drafted him — and who had yet to report.

Three years ago, Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins popped an Achilles tendon two days before the deadline, forcing the Vikings to scramble at the deadline to do a deal with the Cardinals for quarterback Josh Dobbs.

Absent a multi-week injury to a starting quarterback on a contender that doesn’t believe its backup can hold down the fort, the Vikings may be the only team that wants Jones at the deadline.

The preferences of Daniel Jones become a factor, too. If (as we firmly believe) he’s not happy that the Colts folded the tents by trading guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner after a 2-5 start that included an overtime loss to the Chiefs and a toe-to-toe battle with the then-unbeaten Vikings, Jones would have a clear interest in hopping to a contender.

The Vikings wanted to keep Jones after the 2024 season. He opted to sign with the Colts in part because he saw a more realistic path to winning the job over 2023 first-rounder Anthony Richardson in Indianapolis than 2024 first-rounder J.J. McCarthy in Minneapolis. If he’s told that a return to Minnesota would include being installed immediately as QB1, he’d surely prefer that to a lost season with the Colts.

Andd Jones has power over this process. Beyond the basic reality that no team wants a starting quarterback who doesn’t want to play for it, the 2027 roster bonus and base salary that become fully guaranteed in March ($10.51 million) are currently guaranteed for injury. The ESPNFL article mentions that Jones could waive the injury guarantee in order to expedite a deal.

The reverse of that (Jones refusing to waive the injury guarantee) means that Jones could block a trade, if avoiding a potential eight-figure guarantee for 2027 is a dealbreaker for his prospective employer.

Our guess? Right now, only the Vikings currently have interest in Jones. And a trade for Jones becomes a very viable possibility if the Vikings lose to the Bills on Monday with Carson Wentz playing quarterback.

Given the possibility that another team will emerge as a competitor to get Jones, it’s also possible that the Vikings have already decided to trade for Jones after Monday night’s game — win or lose — and that the two teams have agreed to keep it under wraps until Week 9 ends.

Either way, if the oft-injured Jones plays on Sunday against the Cowboys and gets injured, that would kill any chance to trade him. That makes it important to monitor Sunday’s game carefully. If the Colts apply a quick hook to Jones, it could mean that he’s already gone.

#2773. Big Ten standings: What Oregon's win over Ohio State means for College Football Playoff

Big Ten standings: What Oregon's win over Ohio State means for College Football Playoff originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The two preseason favorites in the Big Ten finally went head-to-head in Week 10. Neither of them will leave the game in a position to make the conference title game.

Oregon took down No. 11 Ohio State, 41-28, as Dylan Raiola threw a pair of touchdown passes, while the Buckeyes' offense struggled to keep up behind Luke Fahey.

In a season where UCLA has unexpectedly emerged to become the conference leader, there's been another shake-up in the Big Ten playoff race.

Here's a look at how the Ducks' win will impact the final stretch at the top of the Big Ten.

MORE: Is Ohio State out of CFP race with loss to Oregon?

When Bo Jackson scored his second touchdown of the game around the end of the first quarter, it appeared Ohio State could overcome Julian Sayin's absence to beat an unranked Ducks team fighting to even keep its playoff hopes alive. But a 17-point second quarter — including a gutsy call from Dan Lanning to go for a touchdown instead of a field goal before halftime — changed the game.

Oregon ripped off 31 points in the middle quarters to Ohio State's none, and that was easily enough to prevent Fahey (360 yards, 2 TDs) from making a comeback. The Buckeyes quarterback threw an interception that led to a touchdown and had a fairly modest connection with star receiver Jeremiah Smith (76 yards, TD).

With the win in Columbus, Oregon improved to 6-3 overall and 4-2 in Big Ten play, while Ohio State dropped its second-straight game, also falling to 6-3 and 4-2 in Big Ten play.

MORE:Breaking down Oregon's path to CFP after upset win over Buckeyes

Unexpectedly, UCLA is the clear-cut favorite in the Big Ten in Year 1 under Bob Chesney. The Bruins remained unbeaten in Week 10 by taking down Minnesota, and they have favorable matchups against Illinois and Michigan over the next two weeks.

A West Coast matchup against USC in the last week of the regular season will be the big test for the Bruins, potentially even deciding their playoff fate.

Curt Cignetti's squad remains in a good spot, even with Week 10 off. The key matchup remaining is against USC in Week 11, a game that will likely decide whether or not the Hoosiers will be playing in the Big Ten Championship. A loss could also put Indiana at risk of the committee snubbing them from the field altogether, lacking any key resume wins this year.

The Ducks aren't dead yet. It won't be easy to reach the CFP, as Oregon will need to win out — which shouldn't be difficult against Michigan, Michigan State and Washington — but also get help from Indiana, USC and more to reach the conference title game.

With three losses and a lack of big wins, Oregon likely wouldn't make the CFP as an at-large selection. It will need help to reach the conference championship.

The Trojans have the most potential to cause chaos in the final few weeks of the Big Ten season. A win over Indiana next week, after also beating Ohio State, could put USC in position to claim an at-large playoff bid.

A win over UCLA in the final week of the season could also put USC in position to compete for the Big Ten title. It's a tough schedule break for Lincoln Riley, but even losing one of those two games — leaving USC with three losses — will probably put a pin in his team's playoff hopes.

Unless the rest of the Big Ten contenders fall apart in the next few weeks, the Buckeyes are likely out of the playoff race. No three-loss team has ever made the field, and Ohio State does have a favorable schedule remaining (Northwestern, Nebraska, Michigan), but Ryan Day's team would likely need to get to the Big Ten title game to make the bracket.

Iowa likely won't have enough juice to reach the playoff, but it's not impossible. After the Hawkeyes beat Northwestern on Saturday, they're still hanging around with a light path to 10-2 against Purdue, Illinois and Nebraska over the next three weeks. Iowa's most impressive wins are a one-point victory over Michigan and a shutout of Wisconsin, though, which won't bode well for its at-large bid argument; it's too not hard to imagine the committee picking a three-loss Texas or LSU team over Iowa, considering the SEC schedule.

The Hawkeyes will likely need some help to reach the conference title game, as it's unlikelier that they sneak in as a lower seed due to a lack of big-time wins. At the least, Iowa is putting itself in position to take advantage if other teams crumble.

#2769. Player Personnel Handbook implies that the NFL can delay (or deny) Brandon Aiyuk's reinstatement

Until very recently, people throughout the league believed that the procedure for returning from the reserve/left squad list was administrative, and essentially automatic.

The Brandon Aiyuk case shows that, in the NFL’s view, it definitely is not.

The Collective Bargaining Agreement is silent on the topic of the reserve/left squad list. The relevant language regarding placement (and eventual reinstatement) from the reserve/left squad list appears in the NFL’s Player Personnel Handbook.

In the year when the player is placed on reserve/left squad, he can’t play for his current team or any other team. His season is basically over. The window for reinstatement opens the next year.

Here’s the key language from the Player Personnel Handbook regarding reinstatement: “A player on Reserve/Left Squad must apply to the Commissioner for reinstatement to his club’s Active List. No player on Reserve/Left Squad shall be reinstated in the same season in which he is placed on Reserve. A player applying for reinstatement in a season subsequent to the season in which he is placed on Reserve/Left Squad is prohibited from being reinstated in the last 30 days of the regular season or thereafter during the postseason, and no such player will be reinstated during the period between the trading deadline of a subsequent season and the 30-day deadline unless the club initiates the reinstatement request and the Commissioner approves it.”

While the provision doesn’t say it expressly, the language implies that the Commissioner has apparently unlimited discretion when it comes to approving the application to reinstate the player. In Aiyuk’s case, the Commissioner has dragged his feet since October 27, setting the stage for an apparent effort by the 49ers to leverage Aiyuk’s desire to be reinstated to his willingness to reimburse up to $13 million in previously-paid bonus money.

The NFL Players Association has remained silent throughout the process, and perhaps for good reason. The absence of any provision in the CBA regarding the mechanics of the reserve/left squad list arguably means that the situation falls within the NFL’s “management rights” clause, which allows the various teams “to manage and direct their operations in any manner whatsoever, except as specifically limited by the provisions of this Agreement.”

With no limitations in the CBA as to the operation of the reserve/left squad list (or reinstatement from it), the NFLPA may be without options.

Precedent becomes relevant to the overall analysis. How has the league handled past requests for reinstatement from the reserve/left squad list? If the league has previously not delayed reinstatement (for whatever reason), there’s an argument to be made that it should not be delayed as to Aiyuk.

Regardless, it’s becoming increasingly obvious that the NFL and the 49ers are working together to tie Aiyuk’s reinstatement to his satisfaction of the debt that the 49ers believe Aiyuk has incurred through his prior default under his contract. It should be two separate issues, with the 49ers having the ability to pursue the recovery of bonus money from Aiyuk and Aiyuk having the ability to be reinstated. By tying the two together, the 49ers have found a way to condition Aiyuk’s reinstatement on his willingness to wire a significant payment to the 49ers.

Can the NFL and the 49ers do that? For now, they are. The question is whether Aiyuk and/or the NFLPA can come up with a legal argument against the obvious effort to block Aiyuk’s return until he returns millions to the 49ers.

If Aiyuk wants to be reinstated quickly, his best (and perhaps only) play will be to return millions to the 49ers, with the ensuing goal of earning it back as his career continues elsewhere.

#2768. Center Grove finds its footing, makes Carroll earn third straight state championship

INDIANAPOLIS - The two-time defending state champion Fort Wayne Carroll Chargers were in complete control Saturday night, and then the Center Grove Trojans remembered who they were.

On the verge of getting swept during the IHSAA Class 4A volleyball state finals inside Gainbridge Fieldhouse, the Trojans flipped the switch to force four sets, and their last stand began as the magnitude of the situation finally sank in.

Down 2-0 (25-16, 25-18) against top-ranked Carroll (36-1) in downtown Indianapolis, No. 6 Center Grove found their attacking efficiency in the third set and let their competitive fire breathe life.

"In that third set, we just started playing together as a team, and we all came together during the second set, and were like, this is it," Center Grove sophomore outside hitter Gabby Gilliard said. "We got to play our hardest. We got to put everything out there, and I think in the third set they were underestimating us."

The Chargers rightfully assumed the match was over, leading 17-11 with eight points needed to end the formality of their probable three-peat championship finale.

And then, Gilliard found openings for kills. Senior setter Annabelle Schembra kept setting up her hitters with 27 assists overall in the match, and the digs started to keep rallies going.

"I knew we could do it. We just weren't clicking early enough, fast enough. We saw a little bit of light, and they started to remember, like, who we are," Center Grove coach Jennifer Gandolph Hawk said. "I think we lost ourselves for a while, and then once we found it, it was fun."

A six-point deficit in the third set turned into a 21-21 tie, marking one of the eight deadlocks the Trojans fought to obtain. The final of three lead changes unfolded into a 25-22 win, ending Carroll's string of five consecutive three-set sweeps this state tournament.

"We weren't tired. We had a lot of energy for the third set, and we played like how we normally play," Gilliard said. "We played without nerves. We played because that was it."

Do or die, and the Trojans weren't going to go down without leaving a scar at least.

Gilliard converted 10 kills in 47 attempts through four sets. Sophomore Anna Smith, another one of Center Grove's talented young hitters, finished with a team-best 11 kills by the end.

Junior Kali Kieninger tallied a match-high two solo blocks. Sophomore Olivia Bastien, Gilliard and Smith had 10 digs apiece.

Even in the fourth set, which Carroll won, 25-17, the Trojans stood tied with the Chargers 10 times and held a two-point advantage, 13-11, before the eventual three-time state champions pulled away for their 3-1 victory.

"We were on a mission to get here, but it was just not our night," Gandolph Hawk said. "It was just unfortunate, but I love the fight that they showed. We could have just folded and left in three. We didn't."

Instead, the team that few believed could reach the state finals showed glimpses of the group that ran through Perry Meridian, Roncalli and Franklin Central to win its own sectional – the program's 38th all-time and 12th straight.

They relied on the grit they showcased to defeat Brownsburg in the Cascade Regional and later Bloomington South and No. 4 Yorktown at the Jennings County Semistate.

"I'm really proud of our team, and I'm really proud of everything that we've done and everything we've accomplished this year," Gilliard said. "This is such a great accomplishment."

Center Grove's state finals appearance was its fourth in program history and first since 2009. The Trojans' lone state title was earned in 2000, but with five sophomores and two juniors on the roster this season, it might not be their last trip.

"I think going into next year, we can do a lot more, and we can give a lot more," Gilliard said. "It just didn't click that this was the end, and I think for a lot of us, it didn't click that this was state. We were playing scared, and we couldn't do that."

It was a lesson learned and a painful farewell to a group of seven seniors that helped raise the bar.

"The senior class was on a mission, and they set the standard and the tone. If this is the bar, I think we have a nice road ahead of us," Gandolph Hawk said. "We have a good, solid youth core coming back, and they know what it feels like to get here, so I look forward to what we can do with that group. I love that the seniors set that standard for them to follow."

This article originally appeared on Indianapolis Star: Center Grove finds its footing, makes Carroll earn third straight state championship

#2767. New York Jets vs Kansas City Chiefs: Five Questions with Arrowhead Pride

The New York Jets are on the road in Kansas City, Missouri on Sunday for the 9th game of their 2026 campaign. They will be facing the Kansas City Chiefs. The Chiefs have lost two straight games after starting the season 5-0.

Previewing this matchup, Maurice Elston, a writer at Arrowhead Pride, was kind enough to answer a few questions regarding the 2026 Kansas City Chiefs.

The Chiefs limited their opponents to 10 points or fewer in three of their first five games, but they have allowed a combined 48 points in the last two games. Are the recent struggles on defense just a quality of opponent issue, or are there bigger problems involved?

I think there are some bigger issues involved, particularly the Chiefs' inability to consistently pressure the quarterback and finish possessions on critical downs.

Seattle converted 11 of 16 third downs and controlled the ball for nearly 36 minutes. Denver only converted 2 of 11 third downs, so the defense improved in that area, but the Broncos went 2-for-2 on fourth down. That continued a trend we have seen against the Chiefs: opposing coaches are willing to be aggressive on fourth down because they understand the importance of extending possessions and keeping Patrick Mahomes off the field.

The lack of a pass rush ties everything together. The Chiefs failed to record a sack against Seattle and produced only one against Denver. They have only nine sacks through seven games, with one of the NFL's lowest pressure and sack rates. When you cannot consistently pressure the quarterback, offenses have more time to find favorable matchups. When you combine that with an inability to finish possessions on third or fourth down, it eventually leads to more plays, more yards and more points.

The quality of the opposition certainly played a role, but the pass rush is a legitimate concern that must be corrected.

The Chiefs' offense had fallen into an average-ish range over the past few years, but this year they are back to being one of the better offenses in the NFL. Is this just the Kenneth Walker effect? What has gone right this year that wasn't necessarily working in recent years for the Chiefs?

The Kenneth Walker effect is certainly one of the biggest reasons for the improvement. The Chiefs had not possessed a truly dynamic running game or a home-run threat at running back in recent years. Walker has 770 rushing yards through seven games, which has already surpassed the season total of Kansas City's leading rusher in each of the previous two years. Kareem Hunt led the Chiefs with 728 yards in 2024 and only 611 in 2025.

Walker's presence has changed how defenses must prepare for Kansas City. They can no longer play light boxes, sit back in coverage and assume the Chiefs will eventually abandon the running game. Andy Reid has also used more under-center formations and play-action concepts, which have created better opportunities for Mahomes.

During the first five games, before Tyquan Thornton's injury, the combination worked especially well. Defenses had to respect Walker in the backfield while also accounting for Thornton's ability to stretch the field. When opponents played zero coverage or crowded the line of scrimmage, the Chiefs had somebody capable of beating them deep.

Walker is not the only reason the offense has improved, but his presence has made every other element more effective. The running game, play-action passing and vertical threat were complementing one another in a way we had not seen from this offense in several years.

Can you give us a synopsis of what the Chiefs' draft class has looked like so far, and what you expect from them as the year goes on?

The first name that stands out is Mansoor Delane. The Chiefs traded up to select him sixth overall, and when healthy, he has looked worthy of that investment. The shoulder injury that has followed him since the offseason has caused him to miss time, but his coverage has been excellent. Even on some of the receptions he allowed against Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Delane was in good position. Sometimes a great throw and catch simply beat great coverage.

R Mason Thomas has also flashed as a pass rusher. His sack total does not reflect it yet, but you can see his natural ability to turn the corner and defeat offensive tackles. His next step is learning how to finish those pressures and turn them into sacks.

Emmett Johnson has contributed in several different roles. He has returned kicks, played on special teams and shown value as a receiving and pass-protecting back. His breakout performance against Denver—143 yards from scrimmage, including 128 receiving yards and a touchdown—demonstrated the type of weapon he can become.

Peter Woods, the Chiefs' second first-round pick, has shown flashes but has lacked consistency and is now dealing with a neck injury. Cyrus Allen has not received many offensive opportunities, but he has displayed an intriguing ceiling when he has gotten on the field. Fourth-round cornerback Jadon Canady was inactive or used sparingly early in the season, but injuries in the secondary have created opportunities for him. Seventh-round quarterback Garrett Nussmeier is more of a developmental player and has not factored into the offense.

Overall, I would describe the class as solid with a high ceiling. Delane already looks like a potential cornerstone, while Thomas and Johnson have shown they can become significant contributors. As injuries create more opportunities, I expect several members of this class to take on larger roles during the second half of the season.

Every team has a player or two who may be somewhat unfamiliar to other teams' fans but is known as an unsung hero by fans of his own team. Who are the Chiefs' unsung heroes? If possible, give us one player on each side of the ball.

On offense, I would go with Emmett Johnson. Jets fans may be a little more familiar with him after his performance against Denver, but he still is not a household name. Johnson gives the Chiefs another weapon in the passing game and has also contributed as a runner, blocker and returner. He does not need 15 touches to affect a game because he can create a big play whenever the ball finds him.

Defensively, I would choose Christian Roland-Wallace. With L'Jarius Sneed now on injured reserve, Roland-Wallace becomes an important part of the secondary rotation. He has been one of the Chiefs' most improved defensive players and offers the versatility to contribute outside or in the slot. He may not receive much national attention, but he could play a significant role while Kansas City works through its injuries at cornerback.

If you were an opposing head coach, how would you attack this Chiefs team on offense and on defense?

When defending the Chiefs, my approach would be straightforward until Kansas City proves it can consistently beat it without Tyquan Thornton. I would crowd the line of scrimmage to slow down Kenneth Walker, challenge the Chiefs' wide receivers with physical man coverage and trust my front four to win against Kansas City's offensive tackles. Thornton provided the vertical threat that punished defenses for stacking the box. Without him, teams have been much more aggressive about taking away the running game and forcing the remaining receivers to win one-on-one.

When attacking the Chiefs' defense, I would target the linebackers in coverage. If an offense has a dynamic receiving back or tight end, it should look for ways to isolate that player against Kansas City's linebackers in space. I would also remain aggressive on fourth down, because opponents have shown that extending drives can wear this defense down.

The formula is to force Kansas City's receivers to beat press coverage when the Chiefs have the ball, then use running backs and tight ends to attack the middle of the field when facing their defense.

#2766. Cam Jordan will become third defensive player to play 250 games with same team

When the Saints host the Browns on Sunday, New Orleans defensive end Cam Jordan will reach a rare milestone.

The Week 9 game will be Jordan’s 250th. Via NBC Sports research, Jordan will become only the third defensive player in NFL history to play 250 or more games with the same team.

The others are Darrell Green, who played 295 games for Washington from 1983 through 2002, and Jim Marshall, who played 270 games for the Vikings from 1961 through 1979.

Jordan, the son of former Vikings tight end Steve Jordan, was a first-round pick in 2011. His dad played in 176 games from 1982 through 1994.

Cam is an eight-time Pro Bowler, with 132.0 career sacks. He’s currently 22nd on the all-time list.

#2764. 2. Bundesliga: Dresden off the bottom with convincing victory over Fürth

First half goals from Robert Wagner and Ben Bobzien had the hosts firmly in control at the half. Vincent Vermeij added a second-half strike to make it 3-0 before Hendry Blank saw red for the visitors capping off a miserable evening for Fürth. Dresden made a lively start at the Rudolf-Harbig-Stadion, although Greuther Fürth initially looked dangerous going forward. The visitors came close to opening the scoring through Omar Sillah, whose effort drifted narrowly wide after a defensive mix-up, before Sacha Bansé tested Lennart Grill with a powerful effort from distance. Dynamo also threatened at the other end, with Patrice Čović missing a promising opportunity from inside the penalty area.

However, it was the hosts who eventually broke the deadlock in the 31st minute. Niklas Hauptmann did well to turn away from two opponents before laying the ball into the path of Robert Wagner, whose first-time effort took a deflection off Hendry Blank and wrong-footed goalkeeper Florian Hellstern.

Dynamo doubled their advantage ten minutes later, with Ben Bobzien finding the net in similarly fortunate circumstances. After receiving the ball from Tobias Raschl, the forward cut inside before seeing his effort deflected by Blank and loop into the top corner, leaving Hellstern with little chance of making a save.

Fürth almost reduced the deficit before the interval, with Sillah narrowly missing a cross from Gian-Luca Itter before the latter saw two efforts blocked and deflected wide. Despite those opportunities, Thomas Stamm's side headed into the break with a deserved two-goal advantage.

The hosts continued to apply pressure after the restart and effectively put the contest beyond doubt in the 55th minute. Bobzien turned provider this time, setting up Vincent Vermeij, who had the simple task of rolling the ball into an unguarded net to make it 3-0.

Fürth's evening then went from bad to worse seven minutes later when Blank received his marching orders. Having already been booked in the opening minute, the defender brought down Bobzien as he threatened to break through on goal, receiving a second yellow card and leaving the visitors with ten men for the remainder of the contest.

Dresden looked increasingly comfortable against their numerical disadvantage, with Čović coming close to adding a fourth in the 73rd minute, only for his effort to be blocked by Krisztián Keresztes close to the goal line.

The hosts ultimately saw out a convincing 3-0 victory, recording another impressive home result following their recent wins over Magdeburg and in the cup against Schalke. The three points also provide a significant boost to Dresden's hopes of climbing away from the bottom of the 2. Bundesliga table, while Fürth will be disappointed with an evening in which defensive misfortune and Blank's dismissal contributed to a heavy defeat.

#2763. Intriguing players to watch in Falcons vs. Bengals

The Atlanta Falcons square off against the Cincinnati Bengals in Madrid, desperate for a win to keep their playoff hopes alive after a heartbreaking loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. They'll need several offensive players to bounce back from last week's loss, and others to step up in critical matchups if the Falcons want to be celebrating a win on the flight home.

Quarterback Michael Penix most needs a rebound game after playing the worst game of his career, tossing an uncharacteristic four interceptions against the Bucs. Penix has generally done an excellent job protecting the football and limiting negative plays throughout his career, so last week's performance feels like an outlier.

With Penix promising he'll "shake back" after last week's loss, seeing how that plays out on Sunday morning in Madrid will go a long way toward showing his resiliency as a passer. His injury history has made him resilient through the physical and mental hurdles of playing quarterback, so this should be another test.

Falcons star running back Bijan Robinson has also been uncharacteristically underwhelming in recent weeks, admitting as much this week. After a dominant start, Robinson still leads the NFL in rushing, but the Falcons desperately need him to return to that early-season dominance against the Bengals. A key part of the Falcons' strategy to slow down the Bengals' high-scoring offense will be keeping it sidelined by controlling the clock with Bijan and the run game.

Robinson is still capable of dynamic, explosive runs, but the blown protections on blitz pickups and dropped passes have been some of the areas where he has missed the mark recently. Shining in front of an international audience may be the spark that gets Bijan back to his usual brilliance.

Center Ryan Neuzil will face one of the toughest assignments in Madrid when he takes on Bengals defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence, who is off to a brilliant start this season. Neuzil and the rest of the Falcons' interior offensive line will literally have their hands full against the 350-pound nose tackle. Lawrence is too good to be completely neutralized, but the Falcons must keep him from consistently wrecking the game. That'll be important for their success not only in establishing the run with Robinson, but also in protecting Penix.

Another marquee matchup will be that between cornerback A.J. Terrell and Bengals wideout Ja'Marr Chase. It represents a rematch from the 2020 National Championship game, when both were still at Clemson and LSU, respectively. Chase finished that game with 221 receiving yards and two touchdowns, most of which came at Terrell's expense. That game alone led many to criticize the Falcons for "reaching" on Terrell in the 2020 NFL Draft, and Terrell has worked hard to silence his doubters since.

It's unlikely Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich will make the same mistake Clemson did six years ago: leaving Terrell on an island against Chase this go-round. But Terrell will likely find himself matched up with Chase often on Sunday morning, and if the Falcons want to slow down this high-flying Bengals aerial attack, this rematch will need to be a lot less lopsided.

Speaking of revenge, Falcons safety Jessie Bates likely will enter Sunday's matchup with a chip on his shoulder facing his former team. Bates spent four years in Cincinnati, and that experience could be an X-factor in the Falcons slowing down the NFL's second-highest scoring offense. But that familiarity goes both ways, as quarterback Joe Burrow is very much aware of Bates' propensity to take the ball away. Yet, the better the opposing quarterback, the better Bates tends to play. Three of his last four interceptions have come against MVP candidates Brock Purdy, Matthew Stafford, and Drake Maye. If Bates can add another notch to his belt, the Falcons could add another upset win to their 2026 accolades.

These five Falcons could have a critical impact on Sunday's game in Madrid and determine whether it's time for a fiesta or siesta on the flight home as the Falcons' 2026 season reaches the midpoint. Can you name any other Falcons that intrigue you in this matchup?

#2762. Tennessee Ends Kentucky’s Winning Streak

The Kentucky football team has been one of the darlings of the 2026 college football season. Coming off their bye week, Will Stein's club entered Saturday riding a six-game winning streak. In addition, they sat sixth in the first college football playoff rankings. That's the highest they've ever been. However, they faced a daunting task heading to a place where they've had little to no success. Unfortunately for the BBN, about everything that could go wrong did. As a result, the Cats dropped from a first-place tie. It wasn't pretty, but let's break it down as Tennessee ends Kentucky's winning streak 34-6.

After punting on their first drive, the Kentucky offense had a good chance at getting on the board. However, on a third and eight from the Tennessee 39, Kenny Minchey was picked off in the end zone, ending UK's scoring chances. It was the UK signal caller's first interception since the Alabama game in week two.

The Kentucky defense held once again, and for most of the first quarter neither team got anything going on offense. That was until the end of the period. Daune Morris found a seam against a Kentucky blitz and was off to the races, 66 yards for a touchdown. From there, both teams traded field goals and it was 10-3 Volunteers.

Kentucky's second turnover of the half, a fumble by CJ Baxter, gave the Vols good field position. However, the Kentucky defense held again, allowing no points. Right before the intermission, the Wildcats had their best drive of the game.

Starting at their own four-yard line, Minchey marched the Cats down to the Tennessee seven. A third down throw to all-SEC tight end Willie Rodriguez fell incomplete. Unfortunately for the BBN, they got a no-call of what looked like pass interference, which forced another field goal, making it 10-6 at the half.

Considering how poorly Kentucky had played, you had to feel good about the second half. However, you would be wrong as Tennessee ended Kentucky's winning streak 34-6.

In each of Kentucky's three straight SEC road wins, they trailed in the second half. There was no reason to think it couldn't happen again. But playing in Neyland Stadium has always been rough for Kentucky, and this was no different.

UT got a field goal to start the half, and then the Cats fell off the cliff. A Minchey fumble led to a touchdown pass from backup quarterback Faizon Brandon to Mike Matthews, and just like that it was 20-6. On the next series, Minchey was sacked on a fourth and one at midfield. Tennessee took advantage again as Desean Bishop took it in from five yards out, and the lead was 21.

Kentucky turned it over on downs once again when it appeared Minchey forgot it was fourth down and threw it away. Tennessee took advantage again on another touchdown run by Bishop, and that was your game. We talked in our game preview about how coach Josh Heupel would rely on Bishop, and that was certainly true as he rushed for 109 yards and two touchdowns. Put it all together and Tennessee ends Kentucky's winning streak 34-6.

With the win, Tennessee goes to 7-2 on the season and 4-2 in the SEC. They now have wins over the fifth (Alabama) and sixth-ranked teams in the playoff standings. With so many teams losing on Saturday, will that be enough to squeeze them into the top 12? They travel to Texas A&M next week, and you could make the case they'll be favored in each of their final games.

On the other side of the ball, Kentucky drops to 7-2 and 5-2 in league play. Their six-game winning streak comes to a screeching halt. They return home to Kroger Field to host Florida next Saturday night. UK has won four of the last five from the Gators. They will most likely drop in our bowl projections and playoff rankings.

During the Mark Stoops era at Kentucky, much was made of the so-called "Bye Week Blues" in which the Cats played horribly and most times lost after the week off. At times Saturday reminded you of that. Kentucky looked off from the start and seemingly had no answers against the Vols. However, you have to give Heupel and defensive coordinator Jim Knowles credit. The defense forced three turnovers, had four sacks and eight tackles for a loss.

Kentucky was one of the best in the country in turnover margin, but the Vols flipped that on Saturday. Tennessee only had eight more yards than the Cats (389-361), but going 0-for-2 in the red zone and turning the ball over won't get it done.

At the end of the day, it was another frustrating trip to Knoxville for Kentucky. They've now lost 20 of the last 21 at Neyland with the only win coming back in 2020. Heupel moves to 6-0 against the Wildcats. UK still has a path to the playoff. However, there's no room for error, and they most likely must win out.

Thanks for checking out our recap as Tennessee ends Kentucky's winning streak 34-6 here at Last Word On College Football.

#2761. Cowboys vs Colts: Writer predictions for Week 9

Dallas heads to Indianapolis needing an immediate response after somehow turning a 24-10 fourth-quarter lead into a 33-30 overtime defeat against Arizona. The Colts have problems of their own, losing four straight and entering Sunday at 2-6 after being demolished 42-7 by Jacksonville. This is a game where both teams desperately need something positive before their seasons begin slipping away completely.

There should be no mystery about what Indianapolis needs to try first. Jonathan Taylor has rushed for 610 yards and eight touchdowns, while Dallas just allowed Tyler Allgeier to produce an incredible 147 rushing yards on only 11 carries. After watching Allgeier break runs of 63 and 52 yards, Indianapolis would be foolish not to test the Cowboys on the ground immediately. Taylor remains the best player on this Colts offense and can also contribute as a receiver, so Dallas has to tackle far better than it did during that disastrous second half against Arizona.

The Cowboys' goal should be to stop Taylor and put the game onto Daniel Jones. Jones has thrown only five touchdowns against nine interceptions, while Indianapolis owns the NFL's worst turnover differential at minus-11. The Colts also traded All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson last week, leaving a less experienced offensive line in front of Jones.

That gives Quinnen Williams and the Dallas pass rush a real opportunity after producing five sacks against Arizona. If Dallas can force Indianapolis into obvious passing situations, this is the type of matchup where the defense should finally create pressure without constantly needing to blitz.

Dallas should look at the Indianapolis defense and see an opportunity to rediscover its running game. The Colts are allowing 4.9 yards per carry, and their defensive front no longer includes DeForest Buckner after he was traded to San Francisco. Dallas ran the ball 39 times against Arizona but gained only 93 yards, so simply calling more runs is not enough. Brian Schottenheimer needs to find the concepts and directions that actually create space for Javonte Williams rather than repeatedly running into crowded areas.

Establishing Williams would make life considerably easier for Dak Prescott. Dallas is still scoring 27 points per game, seventh in the NFL, while Prescott has 14 touchdowns against five interceptions. Indianapolis has only two interceptions all season and has just traded away its best interior pass rusher, so there should be opportunities if Dallas stays ahead of the chains.

CeeDee Lamb remains the obvious focal point, although Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward give Indianapolis two experienced cornerbacks capable of making the outside matchups difficult. That makes Jake Ferguson's ankle injury particularly important but he is questionable, while George Pickens was limited by a hamstring issue.

The Cowboys cannot repeat what happened late against Arizona, when the offense had chances to put the game away but failed to finish drives. Indianapolis has conceded 23 touchdowns while scoring only 15 itself, and Jacksonville just put 42 points on this defense. Dallas should attack with balance, use play-action once Williams gets going and force a Colts defense without Buckner to defend the entire field.

Maybe it's just all getting to me, but I'm starting to worry this team is fundamentally and irreparably broken. It feels good like the collapse will continue. Colts 30 Cowboys 27

The Cowboys play the Indianapolis Colts every four years, so the last win at Lucas Oil Stadium feels like a lifetime ago.

If you go back and watch that game, I think this Sunday could have a similar formula. The Colts can't get going on offense and have multiple turnovers, but stick around until the very end.

The Cowboys need to decide whether they're a pass team or a run team and stick to that identity. Flipping back and forth is what's causing this inconsistency.

It's close, but if this Cowboys team can't beat this version of Indy, all hope is lost. I think the Cowboys win 33-24.

The floundering Cowboys take on the fire sale Colts this week. As of this prediction, Jonathan Taylor is still wearing white and blue. If that holds true, he'll be the target to eliminate on Sunday. After watching Tyler Allgeier make swiss cheese of the run defense, forgive me if I lack confidence in their ability to limit the Colts running back. Still, the pattern suggests Dallas will win this one. So with a big sigh and shrug, give me the Cowboys 31-24.

I am very worried that this Cowboys team is broken upon repair. If this is the case, Sunday's matchup against the Colts could end up being the lowest point of an already very low season. I have no confidence this team will show any fight or bounce back, even in a very winnable matchup. I hope I'm wrong, but I see this game being the culmination of the downward spiral as Dallas hits an even lower rock bottom. Give me Indy, 33-20.

Dallas should bounce back this weekend (well that's what I'm hoping), and this matchup against Indianapolis gives them the perfect opportunity to do it. The Cowboys rank seventh-best in the NFL in points per game, while the Colts have the league's worst defenses, allowing 28 points per game. The Colts have also struggled offensively, with Daniel Jones throwing nine interceptions to just five touchdowns. I'm expecting a positive outlook from Dallas and a much-needed victory to get their season moving in the right direction with the Cowboys winning 31-17. Or maybe I'm just being stupidly optimistic.

#2760. ‘We had a chance’: Lane Kiffin baffled after LSU loss to Alabama

The No. 14 LSU Tigers moved the ball up and down the field against No. 5 Alabama on Saturday night, outgaining the Crimson Tide by 172 yards in Baton Rouge. But that didn't matter much on the scoreboard, as LSU fell 31-13 for its third loss of the season.

After the game, head coach Lane Kiffin admitted that he was struggling to make sense of it. Kiffin pointed to some impressive individual numbers from his offense and said he couldn't believe they only added up to 13 points, calling the loss "really disappointing."

LSU entered the season with national title expectations in Kiffin's first year in Baton Rouge, after he rebuilt the roster through the transfer portal. But the Tigers had already lost twice entering Saturday's game against Alabama, including an emotional loss to Ole Miss, Kiffin's former team, and an overtime loss at Kentucky.

On Saturday, LSU went 0-for-4 on fourth down, the most attempts without a conversion in Kiffin's career. The Tigers also made four trips to the red zone and came away with just one touchdown and one field goal.

LSU briefly took the lead late in the third quarter, but Alabama answered with a 32-yard punt return by Ryan Coleman-Williams. On the next play, Keelon Russell hit Cederian Morgan for a 25-yard touchdown, and the Crimson Tide scored the final 21 points of the game.

The loss dropped LSU to 6-3, and its chances of making the College Football Playoff fell from 51% to 25%, according to ESPN's Allstate Playoff Predictor.

After the game, Kiffin pointed out that his offense put up plenty of yards, but it didn't translate to points.

"I was looking at a sheet and it said Sam [Leavitt] had 380 yards passing and Jackson Harris had 11 [receptions] for 166 [yards] and Trey'Dez [Green] had 10 [receptions] for 85 [yards]. I wouldn't think that would equal 13 points," Kiffin said, via ESPN's Alex Scarborough. "But you got to score touchdowns in the red zone."

When asked what's keeping his team from making winning plays, Kiffin didn't have much of an answer.

"I don't know," he said. "We had a chance."

Kiffin also admitted that he didn't expect LSU to be 6-3 at this point in the season, and things won't get any easier next week, as LSU hosts Arch Manning and a Texas team coming off a controversial win over Missouri.

"No, I did not think that, but it is where we are, and we can't change that. So, we got to go back to work. Don't have time to sit around and feel bad. Got a top-10 team coming in here in Texas," Kiffin said.

"It's one thing, probably the one good thing about playing these types of teams in a row like this, 'Hey, you got a chance to play another national game and get back on track,'" he added.
