#2758. Chris Mara tells The Post what’s changed with J.J. McCarthy — two years after Giants passed on QB in draft

Two years ago, the Giants had a chance to select a potential franchise quarterback in the top 10 of the NFL draft.

Instead of taking J.J. McCarthy, the Giants picked receiver Malik Nabers sixth overall before taking QB Jaxson Dart late in the first round.

But McCarthy, thanks to Dart's season-ending knee injury, ended up in New York after all this fall. Chris Mara, the Giants' senior vice president of player personnel and brother of team CEO John Mara, spoke exclusively with The Post's Steve Serby this week and explained what's changed about McCarthy since he entered the draft in 2024.

"We had him rated very high from a skill set. … We weren't quite sure about the maturity level, but we loved his skill set," Mara said. "He showed the ability to win, the ability to lead. Seeing him three years later, this is a completely different-looking person for me."

J.J. McCarthy looks for an open receiver during a Giants' Week 6 loss to the Saints at MetLife Stadium. Bill Kostroun for NY Post

McCarthy was selected 10th overall by the Vikings and missed what would have been his entire rookie season because of injury. When he did return in 2025, he had a roller-coaster season, finishing with a 6-4 record but completing just 57.3 percent of his passes with 11 touchdowns against 12 interceptions.

He fell to third-stringer duty behind newcomer Kyler Murray and veteran Carson Wentz this year, and after Dart's injury, the Giants swooped in to get McCarthy for a fifth-round pick.

In just three games, McCarthy looks more like the quarterback who helped lead Michigan to a national title during the 2023-24 campaign. He's upped his completion percentage to 63.3 and has a 95.2 passer rating, over 22 points higher than last year's mark.

J.J. McCarthy walks off the field after the Giants' Week 6 loss to the Saints. Robert Sabo for NY Post

Giants senior personnel consultant Chris Mara speaks after John Harbaugh's introductory press conference as the team's new head coach on Jan. 20, 2026 in East Rutherford, N.J. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

"On the field and off the field," Mara said about how McCarthy has matured. "He's a terrific guy, he's matured, he's married now, has a kid. I'm in awe when I watch him in practice. He's got a much better arm than I thought he ever had. He moves around great. Listen, the arrow's up on him, too."

McCarthy married longtime girlfriend Katya Kuropas in April. The couple welcomed their son, Rome, in September 2025.

His next big task is taking on the Eagles on Sunday in Philadelphia, a place where the Giants have not won since Oct. 27, 2013.

#2755. Player Personnel Handbook implies that the NFL can delay (or deny) Brandon Aiyuk's reinstatement

Until very recently, people throughout the league believed that the procedure for returning from the reserve/left squad list was administrative, and essentially automatic.

The Brandon Aiyuk case shows that, in the NFL's view, it definitely is not.

The Collective Bargaining Agreement is silent on the topic of the reserve/left squad list. The relevant language regarding placement (and eventual reinstatement) from the reserve/left squad list appears in the NFL's Player Personnel Handbook.

In the year when the player is placed on reserve/left squad, he can't play for his current team or any other team. His season is basically over. The window for reinstatement opens the next year.

Here's the key language from the Player Personnel Handbook regarding reinstatement: "A player on Reserve/Left Squad must apply to the Commissioner for reinstatement to his club's Active List. No player on Reserve/Left Squad shall be reinstated in the same season in which he is placed on Reserve. A player applying for reinstatement in a season subsequent to the season in which he is placed on Reserve/Left Squad is prohibited from being reinstated in the last 30 days of the regular season or thereafter during the postseason, and no such player will be reinstated during the period between the trading deadline of a subsequent season and the 30-day deadline unless the club initiates the reinstatement request and the Commissioner approves it."

While the provision doesn't say it expressly, the language implies that the Commissioner has apparently unlimited discretion when it comes to approving the application to reinstate the player. In Aiyuk's case, the Commissioner has dragged his feet since October 27, setting the stage for an apparent effort by the 49ers to leverage Aiyuk's desire to be reinstated to his willingness to reimburse up to $13 million in previously-paid bonus money.

The NFL Players Association has remained silent throughout the process, and perhaps for good reason. The absence of any provision in the CBA regarding the mechanics of the reserve/left squad list arguably means that the situation falls within the NFL's "management rights" clause, which allows the various teams "to manage and direct their operations in any manner whatsoever, except as specifically limited by the provisions of this Agreement."

With no limitations in the CBA as to the operation of the reserve/left squad list (or reinstatement from it), the NFLPA may be without options.

Precedent becomes relevant to the overall analysis. How has the league handled past requests for reinstatement from the reserve/left squad list? If the league has previously not delayed reinstatement (for whatever reason), there's an argument to be made that it should not be delayed as to Aiyuk.

Regardless, it's becoming increasingly obvious that the NFL and the 49ers are working together to tie Aiyuk's reinstatement to his satisfaction of the debt that the 49ers believe Aiyuk has incurred through his prior default under his contract. It should be two separate issues, with the 49ers having the ability to pursue the recovery of bonus money from Aiyuk and Aiyuk having the ability to be reinstated. By tying the two together, the 49ers have found a way to condition Aiyuk's reinstatement on his willingness to wire a significant payment to the 49ers.

Can the NFL and the 49ers do that? For now, they are. The question is whether Aiyuk and/or the NFLPA can come up with a legal argument against the obvious effort to block Aiyuk's return until he returns millions to the 49ers.

If Aiyuk wants to be reinstated quickly, his best (and perhaps only) play will be to return millions to the 49ers, with the ensuing goal of earning it back as his career continues elsewhere.

#2750. Could Luka Doncic average 40 points for season? ‘You never know’

The 2026-27 NBA season may still be in its early stages, but Luka Dončić's historic start is putting his name in the history books.

And while the Lakers still have 72 regular-season games left, the Slovenian superstar is on the trajectory to achieve a feat none of the league's great scorers have accomplished over the last 64 years.

Luka Doncic (77) of the Los Angeles Lakers hushes the crowd after sinking a three pointer against the Utah Jazz during the second half of their game at the Delta Center in Salt Lake City, Utah, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Getty Images

With his season-high 53 points in Friday's home win over the Trail Blazers, Dončić has scored 361 points through his first nine games of the season, which is the most by a player through their first nine games since Wilt Chamberlain (472 points) in 1962-63. Chamberlain also scored 455 points to open the 1961-62 season.

Chamberlain ended those seasons with scoring averages of 50.4 (1961-62) and 44.8 (1962-63), which are the highest marks in NBA history.

Dončić enters Sunday's road game against the Pistons, which he's questionable for because of low back tightness, averaging a league-best 40.1 points.

Chamberlain is the only player in league history to average at least 40 points for a season.

The closest anyone else has gotten was Jordan at 37.1 points in 1986-87. Harden (36.1 in 2018-19), Rick Barry (35.6 in 1966-67) and Bryant (35.4 in 2005-06) are the only other players in league history to average at least 35 points for a season.

Could Luka Doncic join Wilt Chamberlain as the lone players to average at least 40 points for a season? NBAE via Getty Images

Dončić's career-high scoring average for a season is 33.9 points, which he set in 2023-24 while with the Mavericks. He averaged 33.5 points in 2025-26 in his first full season with the Lakers.

But with the start to the season he's gotten off to, it begged the question: Could he join Chamberlain as the lone players to average at least 40 points for a season?

"It's obviously a long season," Dončić said. "We're just 10 games in. We got 72 left. But as long as we win, I'm good. Hopefully it continues, but you never know."

The answer to that question won't be known until the season is over.

But with Dončić being one of the most prolific scorers in league history, the possibility can't be ruled out.

#2749. FOOTBALL: Gaines delivers night of firsts as Claremore beats Collinsville for second

COLLINSVILLE — It was a night of firsts for Ayden Gaines.

First, the Claremore senior threw his first pass of the season. It went for a touchdown.

Then, on his first carry of the game, he raced 68 yards for another score.

But neither meant quite as much as what happened when the final seconds ticked away Friday night. For the first time in his high school career, Gaines had beaten Collinsville.

During his three years at Oologah, Gaines endured three lopsided losses to the Cardinals, who outscored the Mustangs 124-31 in those meetings.

Gaines accounted for 153 yards of offense and 2 touchdowns as the Zebras defeated Collinsville 26-21, securing second place in District 5A-4 and a home playoff game.

"Oh, it was amazing," Gaines said. "Just the fact that I can get one on them means a lot."

The victory was Claremore's first at Sallee Field since 2013, snapping a five-game losing streak at the venue. The Zebras have now beaten the Cardinals three times in four years after losing seven consecutive meetings from 2016-22.

Claremore coach Jarrett Hurt praised his team's resilience after another closely contested victory.

"It's hard to win over here," said Hurt, whose program is now 15-3 in one-score games since 2023. "Coach [Kevin] Jones and his staff do a super job. They play super defense. They run the ball well, as you can see. It's very difficult to win at Collinsville. They've got a great tradition here.

"I'll tell you what, the best team won tonight, and we had the best player on our team, No. 11, Ayden Gaines. So glad he's a Zebra."

Claremore [7-3, 6-1] closed the regular season with five consecutive victories after a 2-3 start and will host Sapulpa in the first round of the Class 5A playoffs next Friday at Lantow Field.

For Gaines, who never reached the postseason at Oologah, that will bring another career first.

"I'm feeling excited," he said. "I feel like we're pretty evenly matched. We're just going to try to do the same thing we've been doing the past five weeks."

Gaines wasted little time making his presence felt.

On the Zebras' opening possession, he took a direct snap, rolled right and connected with Major Poole-Cain for a 25-yard touchdown pass with 9:45 remaining in the first quarter.

"It meant a lot," Gaines said. "It was the first score of the game. Set the tone. That was a good start for us."

However, Collinsville [5-5, 5-2] responded after a roughing-the-kicker penalty extended its possession.

Quarterback Carter Vaughan found Beau Daniels wide open for a 36-yard touchdown pass, tying the game at 7 with 6:21 remaining. Daniels struck again later in the quarter, scoring on a 22-yard run to give the Cardinals a 14-7 advantage.

But Claremore answered in the second quarter behind a fourth-down gamble.

Facing a critical situation, quarterback Kellen Gaede connected with Jahiem Ewen for a 44-yard gain. Three plays later, Gaede scored on a 2-yard run to tie the game at 14 with 5:11 remaining before halftime.

Gaede completed 9 of 12 passes for 113 yards and rushed for 24 yards and a touchdown on 5 carries.

The Zebras then capitalized on a Collinsville mistake in the closing seconds when Ewen recovered a fumble at the Claremore 32 with 22 seconds remaining. On the next play, Gaines took a direct snap and broke free for a 68-yard touchdown run.

The extra-point attempt failed, but the Zebras carried a 20-14 lead into halftime.

Gaines finished with 72 yards and a touchdown on 3 carries, completed his only pass for 25 yards and a score and caught 7 passes for 56 yards.

His performance continued a remarkable stretch that has gained him recognition as one of the Tulsa World's top-10 players in the region.

"I mean, my whole life is consistent," Gaines said. "[Every time] I wake up for game day, it's the same routine every night and every morning."

Collinsville needed just one play to regain the lead after halftime, with Daniels breaking loose for a 76-yard touchdown run, putting the Cardinals ahead 21-20.

The senior running back finished with 223 yards and 2 touchdowns on 27 carries while adding 2 receptions for 58 yards and another score.

"He's a dynamic athlete," Hurt said. "We've got to stop the run. You've got to be able to stop the run."

Despite Daniels' production, Claremore prevented Collinsville from scoring again.

The Zebras regained the lead when sophomore Kannon Kinnard scored on a 16-yard run with 6:47 remaining in the third quarter. The two-point conversion failed, leaving Claremore ahead 26-21.

Kinnard finished with 107 yards and a touchdown on 25 carries, following his 5-touchdown, 172-yard performance against Pryor.

But his most important carries came in the final minutes.

After the Zebras turned the ball over on downs at the Collinsville 26 with 5:12 remaining, the Cardinals mounted one final possession.

The Claremore defense forced Collinsville into fourth-and-13 at its own 39 with 2:38 remaining, and on the ensuing play, Levi Robinson and Kaden Conley combined for a strip sack of Vaughan, and Preston Hollis recovered the fumble at the Cardinal 37.

Hurt said the defense's priority on Collinsville's final possession was forcing the Cardinals away from their rushing attack.

"We wanted to take away the run and make them throw the football because we thought that was to our advantage," he said. "Turned out we were right."

The Zebras then turned to Kinnard, who delivered consecutive 6-yard runs for a first down, allowing them to run out the clock.

"I'm just glad that they can believe in me because I can go out there and do it," Kinnard said. "It's kind of all like a dream, man. It's crazy out here, but I'm glad because I'm getting to live my dream."

Like Gaines, Kinnard said the victory also carried additional meaning after years of struggling against Collinsville.

"Growing up, I've always been losing to them," he said. "It feels so good to beat them."

Claremore finished with 326 yards of offense, including 188 rushing and 138 passing. The rushing total included three kneel-downs that lost 15 yards on the final possession.

Before those plays, the Zebras had gained 203 yards rushing, averaging 6.2 yards per carry.

"You've got to be able to run the football this time of year in Oklahoma to win football games," Hurt said.

The Cardinals finished with 294 yards, including 219 rushing and 75 passing.

Although Collinsville averaged 7.1 yards per carry, Claremore held it to just 1-of-8 on third-down conversions. The Cardinals did, however, convert 2 fourth downs.

The Zebras also forced 2 fumbles, giving them 7 takeaways over their final two regular-season games against Pryor and Collinsville. That brings the defense to 15 turnovers during the five-game winning streak.

"We preach turnovers all the time," Hurt said. "That's how you win. You've got to create turnovers if you're on defense. That gives you extra possessions. When you've got a guy like Ayden Gaines, you just need a couple of extra possessions, and he's going to do something magical."

The victory also secured Claremore's second-place district finish after the Zebras entered the season projected by some to finish fourth.

Hurt credited the team's challenging nondistrict schedule with preparing his players for close games. All three games against Sallisaw, Bartlesville and Muskogee were decided by one possession.

"We said at the beginning of the year that our nondistrict schedule was going to be the difference," he said. "We lost a couple of those, but I'll tell you what, it's paying off right now. We've won a lot of one-possession games over the years here because our kids have a lot of heart, a lot of character, a lot of grit, and that showed up tonight."

Claremore now turns its attention to Sapulpa [7-3], which finished third in District 5A-3 and enters the playoffs riding a three-game winning streak.

The teams last met in the opening round of the 2023 postseason, when the Zebras escaped with a 48-47 victory after the Chieftains' unsuccessful 2-point conversion attempt. Claremore went on to defeat Elgin 7-6 in the quarterfinals before falling to Del City 34-13 in the semifinals.

A victory over Sapulpa this time would likely set up a quarterfinal matchup against four-time defending Class 5A state champion Carl Albert.

"Our guys have overachieved in a big-time way, according to everybody else, not to us," Hurt said. "So to play at home is huge. We know it's going to be another hard-fought game. They're a very good football team. They've got some outstanding athletes, and we've got our work cut out for us.

"Our theme this year is 'Dream Big,' and we're still dreaming. We're not done yet."

#2747. Cavs’ Kenny Atkinson clarifies his infamous quote vs Knicks: ‘they dominated us’

Kenny Atkinson found himself trending for all the wrong reasons during the Cleveland Cavaliers matchup with the New York Knicks in last year's Eastern Conference Finals.

In case you missed it, here's what Atkinson told reporters after the Cavs were already trailing the series 0-3.

"I think analytically, I think we've won the — I said three out of three [games in the series], we're two out of three in the expected wins, I don't know if you guys follow that — the expected score. We've won two out of three."

Yeah… Cavs fans weren't happy about that.

Jokes have followed Atkinson into the current season. Every loss is followed with a sarcastic rendition of 'analytically, we actually won.'

Atkinson finally had a chance to clear the air before Cleveland's rematch with the New York Knicks on Saturday night.

"I answered the question of 'you're down 3-o, what hope do you guys have?' and I wasn't lying, but in no sense was it like 'oh, we deserve to be winning'; there was zero thought of that," said Atkinson.

It's not easy to give an optimistic spin when your team is trailing 0-3 in a series. Atkinson learned that the hard way.

"I think when you look back on it and take the context of the question, I'm not sure that was taken into account, which was a little bit of a lesson for me," said Atkinson. "I would just say, there was no coach more complimentary of the Knicks and honest about our performance and how they dominated us."

The Cavs were winning in some key expected margins during the series. Particularly in the first two games, where it felt like Cleveland was taking quality shots but just weren't making them. All of that might help you sleep at night — but it doesn't change the end result. Atkinson understands that.

"As coaches, we have to check our process, like, are we getting the right shots?" said Atkinson. "But it kind of doesn't matter, right? Because there's more than that. There is the mental toughness and physical toughness. The flow of the game, how aggressive you are, there's all these other intangibles that go in with that."

#2746. Early domination turns to shutout depression for Detroit Red Wings

DENVER – What an aggravating evening for the Detroit Red Wings. They did so many things right at the start, dominating their opponent on their ice, only for it all to go to waste amid a sea of penalties and punches.

Their old rival, the Colorado Avalanche, scored twice during a penalty-filled second period on Saturday, Nov. 7, at Ball Arena, too much of a lead for the Wings to overcome against such a good opponent. The final score was 4-0, the Wings' third straight loss and fourth in five games.

The outing highlighted the difference between the teams. The Avalanche's best – Nathan MacKinnon, Cale Makar, Martin Necas – feasted, combining for 10 points. Daniil Tarasov didn't stand a chance.

YOUTH EFFECT: Gear in stall, place on plane: Young D-men earn respect from Red Wings

The Wings' best couldn't find the net. As the score grew the tempers flared, and midway through the third period, two players neither side wanted to see fight –for the Wings, Moritz Seider; for the Avalanche, their captain, Gabriel Landeskog – brawled, exchancing multiple punches before officials intervened.

The outing was part of a stretch pitting the Wings against some of the top teams in the NHL: The Florida Panthers (who they beat), Tampa Bay Lightning (a loss) and Vegas Golden Knights (also a loss). In both the Lightning and Avalanche games, the Wings struggled on draws, having lost their best faceoff expert when Dylan Larkin left the team Oct. 29 to wait out a trade.

Another healthy scratch for 2023 first-round pick Nate Danielson, with John Leonard subbing onto the third line instead, next to J.T. Compher and Michael Rasmussen. The other lines had Emmitt Finnie with Alex DeBrincat and Viktor Arvidsson, Andrew Copp with Michael Brandsegg-Nygard and Lucas Raymond, and Sheldon Dries with Carter Mazur and Keegan Kolesar.

EURO SPIN: Henrik Zetterberg says Detroit Red Wings did Steve Yzerman dirty

On the back end, Seider paired with Ben Chiarot, Justin Faulk with William Wallinder and Anton Johansson with Andreas Englund.

Brandsegg-Nygard tested Mackenzie Blackwood with a backhand attempt in the opening minute, part of a strong start for the Wings. By the midpoint of the first period, they had a 6-1 edge in shots. It great more lopsided when DeBrincat sprang Finnie for a breakaway, which ended with Blackwood turning away another backhand shot. With four minutes to go in the period, the Wings had a 10-1 edge in shots. After 20 minutes, it was 13-5..

After a penalty-free first period, the second was nothing but ruts to the penalty boxes. Chiarot went off 51 seconds into the period. Four minutes later, it was Wallinder. While he was in the box, Seider and Nazem Kadri got into it behind Colorado's net, landing each a roughing call. Then Faulk was called for interference, at 7:59. While he served that penalty, Necas put the Avs up by a goal when T.J. Hughes' rebound landed right in front of Necas, who had a half-open net with Tarasov sprawled on the ice.

It grew worse. Kolesar took what was the Wings' fifth penalty at 11:01, sending Colorado onto a fourth power play. Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar demonstrated why they're two of the best players in the game. Manning the point, Makar passed to Necas over on the right; he passed the puck right back to Makar, who found MacKinnon in the right circle for a slap shot and a 2-0 lead.

The Wings? They had two shots on net the entire period.

Any chance of a rally faded when MacKinnon and Necas paired up again. MacKinnon won a draw against Copp. MacKinnon got the puck back from Devon Toews, and ripped a shot from the high slot towards Detroit's net. Taraosov stopped that, but the puck bounced loose and landed in the paint for Necas to finish the play before Chiarot could get to it.

Makar made it 4-0 while the Wings were shorthanded for the fifth time.

The Wings continue their four-game road trip with a move to the east and a stop in St. Louis to face the Blues on Tuesday, Nov. 10 (8 p.m., TNT). The Blues lost Saturday to Nashville on the road – their third straight loss to drop them below .500. St. Louis' last victory? That came back on Oct. 31 when the Blues brought the trick, rather than a treat, to Little Caesars Arena with three unanswered goals in less than five minutes in the third period. After their stop at "The Gateway to the West," the Wings continue moving eastward with a return to Florida, visiting the Panthers on Nov. 12 and the Lightning on Nov. 14. The Wings finally return home on Nov. 18 for an Original Six game against the Boston Bruins on national TV.

Contact Helene St. James at Hstjames@freepress.com. Read more on the Detroit Red Wings and sign up for our Red Wings newsletter.

#2742. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#2741. Early domination turns to shutout depression for Detroit Red Wings

DENVER – What an aggravating evening for the Detroit Red Wings. They did so many things right at the start, dominating their opponent on their ice, only for it all to go to waste amid a sea of penalties and punches.

Their old rival, the Colorado Avalanche, scored twice during a penalty-filled second period on Saturday, Nov. 7, at Ball Arena, too much of a lead for the Wings to overcome against such a good opponent. The final score was 4-0, the Wings' third straight loss and fourth in five games.

The outing highlighted the difference between the teams. The Avalanche's best – Nathan MacKinnon, Cale Makar, Martin Necas – feasted, combining for 10 points. Daniil Tarasov didn't stand a chance.

YOUTH EFFECT: Gear in stall, place on plane: Young D-men earn respect from Red Wings

The Wings' best couldn't find the net. As the score grew the tempers flared, and midway through the third period, two players neither side wanted to see fight –for the Wings, Moritz Seider; for the Avalanche, their captain, Gabriel Landeskog – brawled, exchancing multiple punches before officials intervened.

The outing was part of a stretch pitting the Wings against some of the top teams in the NHL: The Florida Panthers (who they beat), Tampa Bay Lightning (a loss) and Vegas Golden Knights (also a loss). In both the Lightning and Avalanche games, the Wings struggled on draws, having lost their best faceoff expert when Dylan Larkin left the team Oct. 29 to wait out a trade.

Another healthy scratch for 2023 first-round pick Nate Danielson, with John Leonard subbing onto the third line instead, next to J.T. Compher and Michael Rasmussen. The other lines had Emmitt Finnie with Alex DeBrincat and Viktor Arvidsson, Andrew Copp with Michael Brandsegg-Nygard and Lucas Raymond, and Sheldon Dries with Carter Mazur and Keegan Kolesar.

EURO SPIN: Henrik Zetterberg says Detroit Red Wings did Steve Yzerman dirty

On the back end, Seider paired with Ben Chiarot, Justin Faulk with William Wallinder and Anton Johansson with Andreas Englund.

Brandsegg-Nygard tested Mackenzie Blackwood with a backhand attempt in the opening minute, part of a strong start for the Wings. By the midpoint of the first period, they had a 6-1 edge in shots. It great more lopsided when DeBrincat sprang Finnie for a breakaway, which ended with Blackwood turning away another backhand shot. With four minutes to go in the period, the Wings had a 10-1 edge in shots. After 20 minutes, it was 13-5..

After a penalty-free first period, the second was nothing but ruts to the penalty boxes. Chiarot went off 51 seconds into the period. Four minutes later, it was Wallinder. While he was in the box, Seider and Nazem Kadri got into it behind Colorado's net, landing each a roughing call. Then Faulk was called for interference, at 7:59. While he served that penalty, Necas put the Avs up by a goal when T.J. Hughes' rebound landed right in front of Necas, who had a half-open net with Tarasov sprawled on the ice.

It grew worse. Kolesar took what was the Wings' fifth penalty at 11:01, sending Colorado onto a fourth power play. Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar demonstrated why they're two of the best players in the game. Manning the point, Makar passed to Necas over on the right; he passed the puck right back to Makar, who found MacKinnon in the right circle for a slap shot and a 2-0 lead.

The Wings? They had two shots on net the entire period.

Any chance of a rally faded when MacKinnon and Necas paired up again. MacKinnon won a draw against Copp. MacKinnon got the puck back from Devon Toews, and ripped a shot from the high slot towards Detroit's net. Taraosov stopped that, but the puck bounced loose and landed in the paint for Necas to finish the play before Chiarot could get to it.

Makar made it 4-0 while the Wings were shorthanded for the fifth time.

The Wings continue their four-game road trip with a move to the east and a stop in St. Louis to face the Blues on Tuesday, Nov. 10 (8 p.m., TNT). The Blues lost Saturday to Nashville on the road – their third straight loss to drop them below .500. St. Louis' last victory? That came back on Oct. 31 when the Blues brought the trick, rather than a treat, to Little Caesars Arena with three unanswered goals in less than five minutes in the third period. After their stop at "The Gateway to the West," the Wings continue moving eastward with a return to Florida, visiting the Panthers on Nov. 12 and the Lightning on Nov. 14. The Wings finally return home on Nov. 18 for an Original Six game against the Boston Bruins on national TV.

The Broncos keep finding ways to win games — especially close games.

#2736. Booker scores 24, Suns outlast Rockets 102-99 for 1st back-to-back wins of season

PHOENIX (AP) — Devin Booker scored 24 points, including seven straight to break a late tie, and the Phoenix Suns held off the Houston Rockets 102-99 on Saturday night.

Booker broke a 95-all tie with a basket with just under 4 minutes left, then hit a 3-pointer to make it 100-95. Another basket with 2:30 left made it a seven-point Phoenix lead, and Houston couldn't come back. Former Sun Kevin Durant missed a 3-point attempt in the final seconds and Phoenix ran out the clock.

Jalen Green had 16 points, Miles Bridges had 13 points and 10 rebounds and Dillon Brooks scored 11 for the Suns, who snapped an eight-game losing streak against the Rockets.

With their victory over Orlando on Thursday night, the Suns have won consecutive games for the first time this season.

Durant led the Rockets with 21 points and 10 rebounds. Amen Thompson scored 17 points, Fred VanVleet had 16, and Jabari Smith Jr. and Alperen Sengun added 15 apiece.

The Suns shot 76% (16 of 21) in the first quarter in building a 35-23 lead. They led by 19 in the second quarter but Houston finished on a 22-3 run to tie it at 47 at halftime. Phoenix was 4 of 19 from the field in the quarter.

VanVleet's jumper tied it with under a minute to go before the break. He had 10 points in the period and 13 for the half. Khaman Maluach had 11 points off the bench to lead the Suns before halftime.

Booker played in his 745th career game on Saturday, passing Steve Nash for third place in Suns history.

#2733. Lakers vs. Pistons Preview: Strength vs. strength

The Lakers (8-2) embark on their first true road trip of the season on Sunday, starting with a stop in Detroit to take on the Pistons (6-2). This is the first contest of a four consecutive games away from home.

Who: Los Angeles Lakers at Detroit Pistons

After a home-heavy start to the season, the Lakers will hit the road for their first road trip of the season, starting with the stiffest test of the slate.

The red-hot start from the Lakers and Luka Dončić offensively has them ranked as the top offense in the league. The Pistons, meanwhile, enter the contest with the best defense in the league, pitting strength vs. strength.

Like Portland, Detroit plays a physical defensive style to try to overwhelm opponents. Offensively, that hasn't deterred the Lakers in either matchup against the Blazers, but Detroit is arguably the best in the league at that style of play, so it'll be a tough test for the purple and gold.

Like the Lakers, the Pistons excel at steals and blocks on the defensive end. However, they are simply average at rebounding, unlike the Lakers, which allows them to close out possessions and bolster their defensive rating.

Detroit allows the third-fewest wide-open 3-point attempts and teams have hit the fewest wide open threes against them in the league. That stat will be put to the test against Luka and Austin Reaves, depending on how they opt to scheme against them defensively.

One area the Lakers could find success is getting to the line. The Pistons put opponents on the line often, ranking 24th in the league in opponent free throw attempts. The Lakers are fourth in the league in free throw attempts per game.

After battling one of the Western Conference's top teams on Friday, the Lakers will have another tough test on Sunday afternoon against one of the East's elites.

It'll be an interesting test for the purple and gold, and another chance to see how they respond to top competition.

Detroit has been off since losing to the Sixers on Wednesday, so this will be a well-rested Pistons team.

After playing in Friday's G League opener for the Coachella Valley Lakers, both Cameron Carr and Bronny James are joining the parent team on the road trip

Luka is a new addition to the injury report with back tightness as he's listed as questionable. It's the same injury that led to him missing a game against the Clippers earlier this season.

Jalen Duran (hamstring strain) remains out for the Pistons while Isiah Joe is also out with a right hip contusion.

#2732. If Tennessee rout of Kentucky doesn't get CFP committee's attention, nothing will

Tennessee football is winning in an old school style that the College Football Playoff committee simply can't ignore.

It's dominant defense. It's a power running game that takes time to break through. And quite frankly, it can look like a boring brand of college football in an era where flashy offense gets more attention.

It perhaps doesn't gain the attention that it deserves, but that perspective should end with this latest performance.

The 16th-ranked Vols (7-2, 4-2 SEC) hammered No. 7 Kentucky (7-2, 5-2) for a 34-6 win on Nov. 7 at Neyland Stadium. It was a close, low-scoring game until UT scored 24 unanswered points in the second half.

If the College Football Playoff committee stay tuned until the end, it should've come away with a newfound respect for UT's unique brand on dominance.

Coach Josh Heupel described it with his frequently used boxing analogy. He said UT delivers "body blows" in the early rounds to weaken its opponents and then lands a knockout punch.

This overwhelming win over Kentucky was similar to how Tennessee beat No. 9 Alabama, 26-10, on Oct. 17. In that game, the Vols pounded the Crimson Tide with a physical style before breaking through with 14 straight points in the second half.

That's significant because wins over Kentucky and Alabama provide Tennessee's best evidence that it belongs in the 12-team playoff, and not by a small margin.

Kentucky was ranked No. 6 in the first CFP poll, and Tennessee was ranked No. 13.

In Week 10, three teams just ahead of the Vols lost. No. 8 BYU lost to No. 3 Utah. No. 10 Ole Miss lost to No. 2 Georgia. And No. 12 Ohio State lost to No. 23 Oregon. Plus, Kentucky should fall behind UT.

That means Tennessee should move up at least four spots when the updated CFP rankings are released on Nov. 10 (9 p.m. ET, ESPN). And it should reignite the debate over whether UT should jump ahead of Alabama (7-2, 5-2), which it beat handily head-to-head.

There wasn't much discussion about the playoff after the Kentucky game. The Vols know they have three games remaining, and they may need to win all of them to ensure a CFP bid.

Next up is a road game at Texas A&M (4-5, 1-5) on Nov. 14 (3 or 3:30 p.m. ET, ESPN).

"We do a good job of staying week-to-week and focus on who we're playing against," quarterback George MacIntyre said. "Obviously, we saw the rankings and that Kentucky was ranked ahead of us. If anything, we use it as motivation. But it's not that big of a deal in the locker room, especially at this point in the season. It'll become a daily topic later in the year."

But this win over Kentucky should demonstrate why Tennessee belongs deep in the 12-game bracket. It's consistent in a way that most playoff teams aren't in this topsy-turvy season.

With a dominant defense, UT has held five of its six SEC opponents to 20 points or less. Only South Carolina made a late surge to beat UT 27-24.

And the Vols always find a way to run the ball effectively, even if the job takes until the fourth quarter. They've rushed for at least 150 yards in five consecutive games. Against Kentucky, 134 of their 240 yards rushing came in the second half.

Tennessee's brand of football might not be as marketable to the CFP committee because it lacks an established star quarterback. For now, MacIntyre and freshman Faizon Brandon are teaming up to get the job done.

The Vols don't have a budding star like Alabama's Keelon Russell or a veteran transfer like Kentucky's Kenny Minchey. But they beat both quarterbacks by sacking them nine times and forcing five turnovers between Russell and Minchey.

If that doesn't earn the respect of the CFP committee, nothing will.

#2730. Ravens film study: Zion Young stepping up after Tavius Robinson injury

The Buffalo Bills handled the Baltimore Ravens 36-10 in Buffalo last Sunday, in a game that quickly went downhill after starting quarterback Lamar Jackson and backup Tyler Huntley both suffered potentially season-ending injuries. Despite the lopsided score, Baltimore's defense showed some signs of life, with two players standing out on tape. Roquan Smith arguably put together his best performance as a Raven, while rookie Zion Young continued to show why he could be an important piece of Baltimore's defense moving forward.

35 snaps | 21 run defense | 14 pass rush | 1 tackle | 1 assist | 1 pressure

Zion Young's box score may not immediately stand out, but turning on the tape reveals the type of impact that makes his long-term outlook so intriguing. Young finished with 1 tackle, 1 assist and 1 pressure while recording a 100% pass-rush win rate on true pass sets. While the statistical production was limited, his ability to affect running lanes, displace blockers and maintain gap integrity was evident throughout the afternoon. Young continues to show that his value extends well beyond traditional box-score production.

One of Young's most impressive traits throughout the season has been his ability to work down the line of scrimmage against the run, and Sunday was no different. On one rep, Young worked laterally down the line and made a key tackle to prevent Josh Allen from sneaking into the end zone. On another, he flashed his physicality and hand usage, displacing a blocker and forcing the running back to redirect into a different rushing lane. Perhaps his most impressive rep came when he engaged two blockers simultaneously and drove both into the backfield, disrupting the timing of the run and allowing the rest of Baltimore's defense to rally to the football.

With Tavius Robinson sidelined, Young is expected to assume a larger role as Baltimore's starting outside linebacker on early downs. His ability to set a firm edge, maintain gap discipline and use his length and power at the point of attack makes him a natural fit for that responsibility. Young has consistently demonstrated the technique, physicality and effort necessary to succeed as an early-down defender. The next step in his development will be expanding his opportunities as a pass rusher, where his power profile and developing arsenal of moves offer intriguing upside. As his workload continues to increase, Young has an opportunity to establish himself as a foundational piece of Baltimore's defensive front.

52 snaps | 25 run defense | 3 pass rush | 24 coverage | 8 tackles | 4 assists | 1 pressure | 1 forced fumble

Roquan Smith arguably had his best performance as a Raven against Buffalo, flying around the field in coverage, flowing downhill against the run and making key tackles both in the backfield and in open space. Smith finished with 8 tackles, 4 assists, 1 pressure and a forced fumble while allowing just 1 reception for 16 yards in coverage. One of the most impressive aspects of his performance was his ability to consistently put himself in position to make plays, showing the instincts, physicality and range that have made him one of the league's premier linebackers.

On one rep, Smith flashed his ability as a power rusher, knocking back a Buffalo offensive guard and driving him into Josh Allen's lap. Against the run, Smith consistently displayed excellent spatial awareness, navigating around blockers to keep himself clean and meet running backs in the hole. On a toss play to James Cook, Smith showed excellent tackling technique and body control to bring him down in open space. His biggest play of the afternoon came on a shot over the middle, where he rallied to the football and punched it loose to force a fumble that Baltimore recovered.

After receiving a pregame speech from Ravens legend Ray Lewis, Smith delivered arguably his most complete performance of the season. His play over the past several weeks has been inconsistent, particularly compared to the standard he has established throughout his career. However, Sunday's performance was an encouraging reminder of the impact he can have when playing with confidence and decisiveness. If Smith can build on this performance, it could go a long way toward helping Baltimore's defense return to form.

#2728. Things you should know about the newest Raptor, Kevin McCullar Jr.

Kevin McCullar Jr. is the newest addition to this Raptors' roster, joining Toronto on a two-way deal earlier this week on November 5th. The former New York Knick is a 25 year old small forward, standing at 6'6" with a 6'9" wingspan.

After being waived from New York to make space to sign Dalton Knecht, McCullar Jr. joined the Raptors. The leader of the Big 12 in scoring in his senior year, he was an All-American on the Kansas Jayhawks before turning pro. In the NBA, his biggest role came in his sophomore year with the Knicks, where he played in 21 games, including a stretch of matchups when Josh Hart went down with an injury.

From our sister site Posting and Toasting, an idea begins to emerge about who he is beyond the stats. Writer Michael Zeno said that the forward exhibited "pure hustle" while being a threat from deep off the catch-and-shoot, with a penchant for picking up some unnecessary fouls.

TORONTO, CANADA – OCTOBER 13: Kevin McCullar Jr. #9 of the New York Knicks handles the ball during the game against the Toronto Raptors on October 13, 2026 at the Scotiabank Arena in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Mark Blinch/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

From his highlights, you see a shooter with good form, someone who can knock it down past the arc while remaining competent closer to the basket. Having spent time in the G League, the Westchester Knicks made a video interviewing him about his personality, on and off the court. He called his stepback his "go-to move", which he said was his main way of independent shot creation.

This offensive toolkit is certainly something that the Raptors require. Being able to play without the ball in your hands, to allow for the Raptors' arsenal of creators to set the flow of the offence, while not freezing up when executive decisions need to be made, sounds like just what the doctor ordered for this Raptors team. Jamison Battle is the teammate comparison that comes immediately to mind; and while the forward has not yet developed the same reputation as a knock-down shooter, his development further him along in that direction.

In the G League, McCullar Jr. averaged nearly 17 points and six assists, along with three stocks per game, showing some two-way capabilities. He'll likely spend a lot of time on the Raptors 905 developing further, and bolstering a team which just lost its first matchup to the College Park Skyhawks this week.

McCullar Jr. could be the next Raptors success story, developing well and making it out of the G-League to become a productive pro. In a situation where it feels like a roster shakeup is inevitable, the Raptors are taking this first step to bolster the team's shooting.

#2727. If Tennessee rout of Kentucky doesn't get CFP committee's attention, nothing will

Tennessee football is winning in an old school style that the College Football Playoff committee simply can't ignore.

It's dominant defense. It's a power running game that takes time to break through. And quite frankly, it can look like a boring brand of college football in an era where flashy offense gets more attention.

It perhaps doesn't gain the attention that it deserves, but that perspective should end with this latest performance.

The 16th-ranked Vols (7-2, 4-2 SEC) hammered No. 7 Kentucky (7-2, 5-2) for a 34-6 win on Nov. 7 at Neyland Stadium. It was a close, low-scoring game until UT scored 24 unanswered points in the second half.

If the College Football Playoff committee stay tuned until the end, it should've come away with a newfound respect for UT's unique brand on dominance.

Coach Josh Heupel described it with his frequently used boxing analogy. He said UT delivers "body blows" in the early rounds to weaken its opponents and then lands a knockout punch.

This overwhelming win over Kentucky was similar to how Tennessee beat No. 9 Alabama, 26-10, on Oct. 17. In that game, the Vols pounded the Crimson Tide with a physical style before breaking through with 14 straight points in the second half.

That's significant because wins over Kentucky and Alabama provide Tennessee's best evidence that it belongs in the 12-team playoff, and not by a small margin.

Kentucky was ranked No. 6 in the first CFP poll, and Tennessee was ranked No. 13.

In Week 10, three teams just ahead of the Vols lost. No. 8 BYU lost to No. 3 Utah. No. 10 Ole Miss lost to No. 2 Georgia. And No. 12 Ohio State lost to No. 23 Oregon. Plus, Kentucky should fall behind UT.

That means Tennessee should move up at least four spots when the updated CFP rankings are released on Nov. 10 (9 p.m. ET, ESPN). And it should reignite the debate over whether UT should jump ahead of Alabama (7-2, 5-2), which it beat handily head-to-head.

There wasn't much discussion about the playoff after the Kentucky game. The Vols know they have three games remaining, and they may need to win all of them to ensure a CFP bid.

Next up is a road game at Texas A&M (4-5, 1-5) on Nov. 14 (3 or 3:30 p.m. ET, ESPN).

"We do a good job of staying week-to-week and focus on who we're playing against," quarterback George MacIntyre said. "Obviously, we saw the rankings and that Kentucky was ranked ahead of us. If anything, we use it as motivation. But it's not that big of a deal in the locker room, especially at this point in the season. It'll become a daily topic later in the year."

But this win over Kentucky should demonstrate why Tennessee belongs deep in the 12-game bracket. It's consistent in a way that most playoff teams aren't in this topsy-turvy season.

With a dominant defense, UT has held five of its six SEC opponents to 20 points or less. Only South Carolina made a late surge to beat UT 27-24.

And the Vols always find a way to run the ball effectively, even if the job takes until the fourth quarter. They've rushed for at least 150 yards in five consecutive games. Against Kentucky, 134 of their 240 yards rushing came in the second half.

Tennessee's brand of football might not be as marketable to the CFP committee because it lacks an established star quarterback. For now, MacIntyre and freshman Faizon Brandon are teaming up to get the job done.

The Vols don't have a budding star like Alabama's Keelon Russell or a veteran transfer like Kentucky's Kenny Minchey. But they beat both quarterbacks by sacking them nine times and forcing five turnovers between Russell and Minchey.

If that doesn't earn the respect of the CFP committee, nothing will.

#2726. Ravens LB Roquan Smith fined for missed penalties vs. Bills’ Josh Allen, DJ Moore

Baltimore Ravens linebacker Roquan Smith had an expensive day in Orchard Park, NY last weekend. Smith received a heavy dose of fines for his on-field efforts against the Buffalo Bills in Week 8. He was fined a total of $35,822 for two infractions, one against quarterback Josh Allen, and a second against wide receiver DJ Moore.

The NFL handed Smith a fine of $17,911 for a facemask grab and tug he implemented on quarterback Josh Allen during a successful touchdown sneak, per Tom Pelissero. During the play, Smith was observed grabbing Allen's facemask while trying to pull him back, then pulling and twisting the helmet aggressively until it ended up completely backwards — and with Allen's head and neck turning almost a complete 180 degrees. Smith wasn't penalized following the play.

Here's a closer look via still shots available from the play:

Smith was also received an additional fine of $17,911 for unsportsmanlike conduct, which the NFL levied as a hit on a defenseless player. Sal Capaccio of WGR 550 noted that the particular play involved Smith hitting Moore as he was "going across the middle in the 1st quarter as the ball was thrown elsewhere."

Many wondered if Smith would face discipline following the now-viral play against Allen. He seems to have avoided suspension despite a pattern of concern, as evidenced by Smith's availability for Thursday Night Football in Week 9, just a few days ago.

Smith is a highly decorated defensive mercenary. This week, however, he's the one taking a huge hit where it hurts — thanks to a decent bit less of the typical $1,176,470.59 he's paid per game in 2026.

#2724. Warriors forward Georges Niang gets a tech after shove war with Magic

SAN FRANCISCO ― Golden State Warriors forward Georges Niang has brought added toughness to the team, and it rears its head often throughout the game.

Niang and Orlando Magic center Wendell Carter Jr. were separated by teammates before being assessed technical fouls a brief push-off and animated words between the two during a regular-season meeting between the Warriors and Magic on Saturday, Nov. 7 at Chase Center in San Francisco.

With 9 minutes and 17 seconds in the second quarter, Carter received an entry pass inside the paint, and Niang, out of position, committed an intentional foul, wrapping up Carter before he could get off the ground.

Warriors forward Draymond Green and guard Gary Payton II de-escalated the situation, protecting Niang.

After officials reviewed the play, double-technical fouls were handed out to Niang and Carter.

Niang has mixed it up with anyone and everyone showing that he's a guy that's willing to scrap, claw and get in opponents face. He won't allow others to impose their will on his team. And when the Warriors want to get physical, Niang is down for the get down.

The type of energy, that type of spunk is what fellow teammate Green raves about. Green has already had to hold Niang back when getting into it with Miami Heat forward Bobby Portis and Los Angeles Lakers guard Collin Sexton.

Niang wasn't on the court during the dust up with Phoenix Suns and guard Dillon Brooks, but he looked on as if he wanted to get in the mix.

"I love that, I love that type of energy, by the way," Green said. "George has been incredible for us and the way he shoots the basketball. Crazy thing is he hasn't even shot it at a level that he shoots the ball at and yet the impact that he's had on this team on every aspect of the game. He's so smart."

Niang is avergaing 7.9 points, 3.1 rebounds, and 1.7 assists per game for the Warriors through nine games. He's a career 39.7% 3-point shooter but has only connected on 30.6% of attempts so far in the 2026-27 season.

Still, it's the little things that Niang does that makes him valuable to the Warriors roster.

"What an addition," Green said. "That's one of those signings that people look at like 'aw man' but then you look up and this guy, you can't keep him off the floor. He's been absolutely great for us. I have absolutely loved being his teammate."

"I'll be honest, I have times (when) I do some random (expletive) out there, especially on the defensive end. But even on offense, and he just picks up on it like that. ... Really fun player to play with."

#2723. Penn State notes: Carson Hansen again shows why his coach believes in him

SEATTLE – Penn State football fans clamored for coach Matt Campbell to replace Carson Hansen in the backfield through the first seven games.

Hansen, however, has shown the last two games why his coach has had such trust and confidence in him.

He carried 14 times for a season-high 119 yards and one touchdown as the Nittany Lions held off Washington 28-25 Saturday at Husky Stadium.

A week ago, he ran 17 times for 96 yards and a TD in a 31-17 victory over Purdue.

"The offensive line has done such a great job the past couple games," Hansen said, deflecting praise. "I just really appreciate them, all the work they put in throughout the week and all the sacrifices that they make as a team.

"There's nothing better than creating memories together."

On Penn State's first drive, Hansen gained 20 yards on a cutback run and then made several Huskies miss on a 12-yard TD. He had a 10-yard run before Rocco Becht's 45-yard TD pass to Chase Sowell in the second quarter.

He capped his afternoon with a 36-yard burst as the Lions ran out the clock on their final possession.

"Carson's always been a player who the more he goes in a game, the better he gets," Penn State coach Matt Campbell said. "I think that's the case with every great running back I've coached. He and Cam (Wallace) are playing with a lot of confidence right now.

"I thought the offensive line did a really great job in the running game. I thought the tight ends were really good as well."

Wallace ran just seven times for 56 yards, including a 46-yard touchdown run in the second quarter. But Hansen received the bulk of the work and finished with his first 100-yard game in a Penn State uniform.

"He took some strides today," Sowell said. "He played his game. He didn't try to think too much or be robotic out there. He let things flow and got into his groove."

Sowell finished with four receptions for 125 yards and a TD, but it was his 36-yard one-handed grab in the third quarter that everyone wanted to discuss.

"I work at it every day," he said. "There are plenty of times they (defensive backs) have one arm and all you got is one arm. It's just being savvy, putting myself in those positions beforehand and having the confidence to make those plays.

"No matter what, I'm going to catch it. You have to tackle me or trip me."

Sowell's status went from probable to "game-time decision" Saturday on the Big Ten availability report. He's been dealing with an ankle injury, which kept him out of the Purdue game last week.

"There was a lot of talk about being smart with the future and all those things," he said. "I'm too competitive. I have to be smart and take care of myself. That's why I sat out the last game. Even that game I wanted to play. They were telling me I couldn't go.

"You have to kill me to take me off the field or I have to be dragged off the field. I got a little ankle and some guys are out there playing with messed-up backs and necks."

Redshirt sophomore Garrett Sexton saw the majority of playing time at left tackle for Penn State in place of Malachi Goodman, who started but who's been dealing with an unspecified injury.

Sexton helped the Lions rush for 174 yards in his most extensive action of the year.

"Malachi has been dinged up," Campbell said. "We just didn't know how long he could go. He was not at full strength. We knew he'd be able to give us some. Garrett really had a great week of practice. I'm proud of Garrett. I thought he did a really good job."

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2720. NFL odds, betting, storylines: 2 underdogs to back in Week 9

If the NFL betting community handed out a first-half MVP award, there is no question who this year's runaway winner would be: big NFL underdogs.

Through eight weeks, seven teams have taken the field as double-digit underdogs. Five of them covered the spread.

So far, we have seen 37 underdogs of six points or more (including those seven double-digit pups). Their ATS record: 24-10-3 ATS.

This includes a 6-2 ATS mark posted by the largest underdog of the week. In fact, the biggest underdog has covered the spread each of the last five weeks and recorded three outright upsets.

All of which brings me to my trio of NFL underdog best bets for Week 9. Spoiler alert: I expect big 'dogs to continue barking.

Malik Willis (No. 2) and Ollie Gordon II could have a surprise in store for the Lions. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images)

After an uneven 2-2 start to the season — a start that included a frantic overtime home win against the Saints, blowout road losses to the Bills and Panthers, and zero covers — the Lions have turned things around.

The bounce-back began with a 45-21 thumping of the Cardinals in Arizona. Detroit then followed its bye with consecutive divisional home wins over Green Bay and Minnesota. Those wins, however, were hardly convincing. The Lions needed a last-second field goal to upend the Packers 20-17 and a late-game touchdown and defensive stop to hold off Minnesota 19-15.

So seven games into the 2026 season, Detroit has defeated just two opponents by more than four points: Arizona and the New York Jets (who lost 31-24 in Motown in Week 3). The Lions also enter Week 8 having covered only two point spreads.

Now they head to South Beach in what is a classic letdown/sandwich spot.

The letdown part: Detroit just barely beat two NFC North rivals in tense, down-to-the-wire games (both of which were at home). Now with their confidence sky high, the Lions hop on a plane to face one-win Miami.

The sandwich part: Detroit next week kicks off a three-game homestand against New England. So this is the team's only road trip over a six-game stretch.

My point is that this is a tricky situation for the Lions. Which means it's an advantageous one for the Dolphins, who have been much more competitive over the past month.

Since opening with double-digit losses to the Raiders, 49ers and Chiefs by the combined score of 86-36, Miami has upset the Jets 28-25 on the road and held its own against the Vikings (15-10 road loss as a 10-point underdog), Bengals (31-24 home loss as a 7-point underdog) and Patriots (24-19 home loss as a 7-point underdog).

Yep, Miami comes into this contest on a 3-0-1 ATS run. And while the defense has admittedly struggled most of the season, the offense has picked it up recently. Since tallying 13, 13, 10 and 10 points in their first four games, the Dolphins averaged 23.7 points in the last three.

If the offense can exceed that average Sunday by a tiny bit — against a Detroit defense that I'm not convinced is fixed — Miami will get inside this big number.

In Week 1, the Commanders traveled to Philadelphia as 6-point underdogs. They lost 24-22.

Two weeks later, with injured starting quarterback Jayden Daniels on the sidelines, the Commanders hosted defending champion Seattle as 8.5-point underdogs. They won 33-31.

Fast-forward to Week 6, and Washington traveled to San Francisco as a 7.5-point underdog on Monday Night Football. The 49ers won — but only by six points (23-17).

Those were the three biggest point spreads the Commanders have faced as an underdog this season. And they covered them all. Now they're catching a bunch of points against the visiting Rams, who have looked much better the last two weeks, thumping the Raiders and Chargers by the combined score of 59-30.

But let's not forget that this same Rams squad preceded those two wins with an 18-16 loss to Arizona as a 12.5-point home favorite. Before that, L.A. suffered an overtime home loss to Buffalo; needed a furious late fourth-quarter rally to win at Philadelphia; and blew a 16-0 halftime lead in a 30-26 loss at Denver.

Back to Washington: True, it got crushed 37-20 at Dallas as a 4.5-point underdog in Week 2. But it lost Daniels to an elbow injury right before halftime.

The Commanders also fell 30-13 to the Colts in London as 5-point underdogs in Week 4. But seventh-round rookie quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis played the majority of that game after backup Marcus Mariota went down early.

Daniels finally returned the following week, which was the now-infamous 27-27 tie against the Giants (who are 4-2-1). Then came the competitive loss at then-unbeaten San Francisco, followed by an off week, followed by last Sunday's 27-10 rout of the Eagles.

Bottom line: The Commanders have been blasted only twice this season — once with their backup QB playing the second half and once with their third-string rookie QB playing the majority of the game. Assuming Daniels can stay on the field for 60 minutes Sunday, I like Washington's chances to hang with a West Coast team traveling across the country to play in the early window.

By the way, the Rams' 14-point victory at Las Vegas two weeks ago? It's the only time they've won by more than four points in their last eight games outside of Los Angeles.

#2718. Elija Lofton's near-catch for Miami becomes latest entry in Canes-Irish rivalry lore

SOUTH BEND, Ind. (AP) — For 38 years, Miami has insisted the same thing: Cleveland Gary didn't fumble in a still-debated loss at Notre Dame.

Add another did-he-or-didn't-he to the lore of the rivalry between the Hurricanes and the Fighting Irish. Miami argued that Elija Lofton caught what would have been a touchdown pass late in the fourth quarter of what became a 31-24 loss to Notre Dame on Saturday night — only to have the referees say Lofton didn't complete the play.

"Very disappointed in the way that was called with the game on the line and clear possession inbounds," Miami coach Mario Cristobal said.

Had Lofton been credited with that catch, it would have made the score 31-30 with an extra point try pending. Miami lost the 1988 game — the one where the Hurricanes say Gary didn't fumble — by that same 31-30 score. And if that wasn't enough of an eerie coincidence, Miami entered that 1988 game ranked No. 1 in the country while Notre Dame came in ranked No. 4.

The rankings going into Saturday night: Miami No. 1, Notre Dame No. 4.

Lofton had the ball in his hands and his feet were down, which was the reason why Miami felt it was a touchdown. But the issue was whether the catch was completed, and Lofton had the ball knocked away by Notre Dame's Luke Talich — while both players ended up out of bounds.

That 1988 loss that still stings Miami because it took away a national title shot. Gary was ruled to have fumbled near the goal line, even though Miami argued he was down before the ball came loose and was recovered by Notre Dame.

"Robbed. We were robbed," former Miami star Randal Hill said of the Gary play.

Miami could have felt the same way on Saturday.

This one doesn't knock Miami out of title contention — the College Football Playoff is still very much in play for the Hurricanes. But the Lofton play, at minimum, is one that fans will debate for a long time.

The fact that Miami had a chance at tying the game late probably surprised some, based on how the first 35 minutes went. The Hurricanes — playing without injured receiver Malachi Toney — got into a 24-3 hole in the third quarter before their comeback push started.

Among all Football Bowl Subdivision players entering this weekend's slate of games, Toney was second with 73 catches, tied for second with 13 touchdown receptions and third with 1,027 receiving yards. He was widely considered to be a Heisman Trophy contender, the most electrifying player on the most dynamic offense in the country.

Toney was responsible for 35% of Miami's catches, 39% of its receiving yards and 46% of its touchdown receptions in the Hurricanes' first eight games. In his absence, Cooper Barkate caught a pair of touchdown passes and Lofton had a TD grab as well — but in the end, the Hurricanes were left to wonder what might have been.

The Cleveland Cavaliers lost to the New York Knicks 109-97. Donovan Mitchell finished with a season-high 37 points.

The Cavs started strong for the second night in a row, showing active hands defensively in the first quarter to force three Knicks turnovers. They also held the Knicks to just 3-of-11 three-point shooting in the opening quarter.

Karl-Anthony Towns kept New York attached. He scored 14 points in the first quarter while throwing down a pair of thunderous dunks. This was a much more difficult matchup for Mobley than the previous night, when he held Joel Embiid to 0-of-9 shooting.

A Knicks run led by Jalen Brunson put New York back in front going into halftime. Brunson hit tough shots en route to 16 points in a five-minute stretch. He finished the first half with 20 points.

Cleveland trailed 63-53 at halftime. Then the Knicks blew it open in the third quarter to extend an 18-point lead into the final frame.

New York's quick-hitting offense, which thrives on off-ball movement and screening, had the Cavs perpetually lost throughout the night. James Harden struggled to navigate screens, while the rest of the Cavaliers (even Evan Mobley) weren't able to communicate cleanly enough to avoid giving up opportunities at the rim.

This proved to be a bad combination for the Cavs in last year's playoffs, and it looks like their personnel still isn't able to keep up with New York's offense.

Towns and Brunson ended with a combined 60 points. The Cavs ended this game needing far more from Evan Mobley and James Harden. The two combined for just 19 points. It felt like Mitchell was the only Cavalier who could find his shot for most of the night.

Of course, the Cavs were without some key players tonight. Jarrett Allen missed his third straight game, while Jaylon Tyson has been sidelined since before Halloween. Sam Merrill, who injured his elbow in Friday's game, was also out tonight.

#2713. Penn State builds big lead, holds off Washington for 2nd straight Big Ten win [updated]

SEATTLE – One hundred and five years ago, the Penn State football team traveled across the country by train to play Washington at Husky Stadium.

Appropriately, the Nittany Lions looked like a runaway locomotive in the first half Saturday and built a 22-point lead in their second game in Seattle.

But the Huskies slowed Penn State's offense in the second half as if they threw gobs of molasses under the Lions' wheels and pulled within three points.

Somehow, though, they collected themselves, held the ball for the final 7:40 and turned back Washington 28-25 for their second straight Big Ten victory.

"It was great to win a football game where everything was going against us a little bit, very reminiscent of the Wisconsin game (a 24-20 loss in September)," Penn State coach Matt Campbell said. "It was great to be able to catch ourselves and win the game."

The Lions (2-4 Big Ten, 5-4) drove from their 25 to a game-clinching first down at the 1 behind Rocco Becht's quarterback sneak on fourth down, Carson Hansen's 36-yard burst and two Washington mistakes.

Becht scrambled for 9 yards on third-and-6 early in the drive and took a hit to the helmet from Washington linebacker Jacob Manu at the Penn State 38. Wide receiver Chase Sowell took offense and bumped Manu, drawing an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty.

The Big Ten crew then reviewed the play for targeting and ejected Manu, which nullified Sowell's penalty.

"Obviously that was a frustrating situation on the personal foul," Campbell said. "But I don't know if it should have gotten to that point. I thought our kids had the ability to re-focus with the timeout."

Two snaps later, Hansen ran off the left side and into open field to the Washington 22. Hansen was then stopped short of the chains on third down, but the Huskies had too many men on the field. That gave Penn State a first down at the 12.

After Hansen's short run, Becht carried three straight times and picked up the first down on fourth-and-1 from the 3 to seal it. He took a knee three times before time ran out.

"We told each other we had a chance to win the game on our terms," right tackle Anthony Donkoh said. "We've been playing with our food all night. Let's end the game on this drive."

The Lions had gained 36 total yards and two first downs in the second half before their monumental drive.

"The last drive was incredible by all those guys," Becht said. "We stayed resilient. We had the urgency and conviction to stay together and run that clock out."

Becht completed 16-of-27 passes for 240 yards and two touchdowns, Hansen carried 14 times for 119 yards and one TD and Sowell caught four passes for 125 yards and one score, including a spectacular one-handed catch for 36 yards in the third quarter.

Defensively, Penn State contained Washington (2-4, 5-4) in the first half before Demond Williams Jr. got rolling. He threw two touchdown passes and two successful two-point conversions to help pull the Huskies within three points.

"I thought we had an opportunity there in the second half," Washington coach Jedd Fisch said. "I was convinced after we made it 28-25 that we were going to get a stop, get a score, win that game and have a pretty remarkable comeback.

"We can't put ourselves in that position."

Williams finished 19-for-33 passing for 172 yards with one interception by Penn State reserve Ibn McDaniels. Linebacker Tony Rojas appeared to sack him in the end zone in the second quarter or force an intentional grounding penalty. But the officials ruled it an incompletion.

Penn State could have taken an even bigger lead in the first half had running back Quinton Martin Jr. been able to catch Becht's pass when he was behind the secondary in the second quarter.

Some might call it an ugly win, but the Lions' flight home was a happy one. They improved to 5-0 against the Huskies.

"I just feel like we're growing in a lot of different areas," Campbell said. "It's awesome to watch the growth happen. Obviously everybody wants the growth to happen instantaneously. The reality is that we are starting to become a real football team and that part is exciting."
